* BACKLOG TASK-099T6 driver_modes equivalence test spawns real claude twice on one session id and now collides    :drivers:test:claude:bug:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-099T6
:PRIORITY: P1
:END:

Found 2026-07-26 running the TASK-8W30B merge gates on main (433fef1 + merge).

SYMPTOM

`cargo test -p orgasmic-drivers --test driver_modes` fails:

    ---- legacy_drivers_and_explicit_pairs_emit_equivalent_start_events ----
    assertion `left == right` failed: legacy=claude-acp mode=acp-stdio harness=claude
      left:  Ready { protocol_version: "claude-code-stream-json/1", ... }
      right: TextChunk { stream: Stderr,
             chunk: "Error: Session ID 6fc90d23-2093-4957-9fa9-ccb9488e0bb1 is already in use." }

CAUSE

The test deliberately shares one identity across the two spawns it compares
(driver_modes.rs:1665-1684, comment: "Share one identity so harness-aware native
metadata (e.g. the tmux claude --session-id pinned to runtime_id) is identical
across the legacy and explicit drivers being compared"). That was harmless while
`--session-id` was computed and then dropped. TASK-SGRTX (f5c6913) and 0f65de5
made the flag actually reach the claude process, so the second spawn of each pair
now asks claude for a session id the first spawn just claimed.

This is fallout from making the claude driver real, not from TASK-8W30B. The
8W30B implementer saw this suite green (28/28) in its worktree and the manager
saw 27/1 on the merged tree an hour later, so it presents as intermittent — the
collision depends on whether the first spawn has registered the session by the
time the second starts. Treat it as a race that is always latent, not as a test
that sometimes breaks.

TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, BOTH WORTH FIXING

1. The equivalence assertion needs identical *metadata* across the pair, not an
   identical live session. Give each spawn its own session id and normalize the
   id out of the compared Ready event, the way `normalize_volatile_ready_event`
   already removes `session_id` at line 1724 — or make the case inert.

2. This test spawns a REAL `claude` process, twice per case. Per the gotcha
   "Asking a harness to prove it can work costs real money", a claude turn cost
   $0.0994 and 24.5k tokens when measured 2026-07-25. A default-suite test that
   bills the operator on every run is a problem independent of the collision, and
   it got worse the moment the driver stopped being inert. Decide whether this
   case belongs behind an opt-in gate.

Acceptance:
- `cargo test -p orgasmic-drivers --test driver_modes` is green on repeated
  consecutive runs, not once
- the claude case either does not spawn a billable real turn by default, or its
  cost is a deliberate, documented choice
- the equivalence property being asserted is still actually asserted
2026-07-27, TASK-RWCRN dispatch: this test is now actively costing money on ordinary gate runs, not just on deliberate invocation. The brief explicitly told the worker not to run it; the worker ran it once anyway and was right to flag why — `cargo test -p orgasmic-drivers` is a declared verification gate and this test is not #[ignore]d, so the gate as written cannot avoid it. It failed on a real claude spawn with "Error: Session ID 377794d3-... is already in use", the documented TASK-099T6 collision, made more likely because the suite ran inside a live claude dispatch. Until this is #[ignore]d, every brief must carry a --skip instruction and every gate run must use `-- --skip legacy_drivers_and_explicit_pairs_emit_equivalent_start_events`, which is exactly the kind of tribal knowledge that does not survive. The manager's own gate run used the skip and was green: 239/4/28/1.

* BACKLOG TASK-0DANB Billing-capable daemon tests are one lock from a charge and their ignore reasons hide the spend    :daemon:testing:mechanism:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-0DANB
:PRIORITY: P2
:END:

Follow-up to TASK-MFJZ7 (merged), which gated the one ungated billing-capable
test and audited the rest. Its audit left four daemon-side items, all
default-safe today via bare `#[ignore]` but out of that dispatch's write scope:

- `real_cursor_agent_stream_json_bridge_emits_events_and_releases`
  (`crates/orgasmic-drivers/tests/cursor_agent.rs:136`) — wait: drivers crate,
  but was left as-is because already ignored; include for wording only.
- `dispatch_endpoint_routes_cursor_agent_through_supervisor_and_emits_run_created`
  (`crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/dispatch_endpoint.rs:994`)
- `dispatch_endpoint_routes_acp_stdio_codex_through_supervisor`
  (`crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/dispatch_endpoint.rs:1060`)
- `dispatch_grace_path_writes_artifacts_without_terminal_session_marker`
  (`crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/dispatch_endpoint.rs:2129`)

Three carry ignore reasons phrased as availability ("requires X installed")
when the real hazard is spend: someone installing codex and running
`--include-ignored` to "check the codex path" gets a charge. `#[ignore]` is a
control, but a single-lock one, and the wording invites exactly the mistake.

=== Ask

1. Extend the MFJZ7 mechanism (`BILLED_TESTS` + `skip_unless_billing_allowed`
   + `report_billed_tests`, in `orgasmic_drivers::modes::rmux::test_tooling`)
   to the daemon test binaries above, so `--include-ignored` alone cannot bill
   without `ORGASMIC_ALLOW_BILLED_TESTS=1`.
2. Reword every billing-capable test's ignore reason to name the spend.
3. Re-run MFJZ7's audit method on `crates/orgasmic-daemon/**` (it audited
   drivers thoroughly; daemon got only the grep-obvious cases): every
   `.acquire(`/harness spawn in daemon tests, verdict per test.

=== Acceptance

- Collection proof both arms (never execution), per the MFJZ7 standard: without
  the env, `--include-ignored --list` collects but the guard's runtime skip is
  shown on a safe representative; with the env, collection shows it armed.
- Audit table recorded on this task.
- A `verify/TASK-<this>/` artifact per the TASK-TCTTD standard — with a patch
  that `git apply` ACCEPTS (MFJZ7's shipped patch was a documentation diff that
  git apply rejects; do not repeat that).

* BACKLOG TASK-0KP3T the stdout-mirror fallback keys on handle presence, not write success: a failed durable write loses the line and wedges the sink for the process lifetime    :daemon:ops:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-0KP3T
:PRIORITY: P2
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/**,verify/**
:END:

** Description
From the TASK-G64ZH.1.1 review (F-1, MEDIUM, non-blocking, PRE-EXISTING).
=logging.rs:573-587=, =:594-601=, =:520=.

TASK-G64ZH.1.1's whole framing is that "do not double-write" must be decided from
whether the durable sink ACTUALLY TOOK THE LINE. The shipped code decides it from
=state.durable.is_none()= — handle PRESENCE, not write SUCCESS. A handle that
exists and whose =write_all= returns =Err= is a live handle that got nothing:

1. =:574= =write_all= fails -> =record_drop()= at =:575=, and THE HANDLE IS
   RETAINED (never set to =None=).
2. =:598= then sees =durable.is_some()= -> stdout suppressed.
3. The line is in no file, on no fd, in no terminal.

AND IT COMPOUNDS: because =state.durable= stays =Some=, =maybe_reopen_durable= at
=:520= short-circuits =true= on every subsequent line forever. No reopen, no
backoff, no recovery — the sink is wedged for the daemon's lifetime.

Trigger class: =ENOSPC=, =EDQUOT=, =EIO= — a full disk, a quota, a failing volume.
Distinct from the open-failure class the G64ZH chain closed, which is why three
rounds of that chain did not reach it.

** Why it was not blocking
Genuinely PRE-EXISTING: identical at =eaa88da^=, before the chain started. It is
the last surviving proxy after four rounds removed the others, and it is outside
every acceptance bullet those rounds were written against.

** Direction
Treat a failed durable write like a failed open: drop the handle so
=maybe_reopen_durable= owns recovery, and let the write-time fallback send the
line to stdout. That reuses machinery TASK-G64ZH and TASK-G64ZH.1.1 already
built. Consider whether =write_all= failure should count toward the same
=dropped_log_writes= meaning the chain just settled on ("one per line that never
landed").

** Acceptance
- A live handle whose =write_all= fails does not lose the line, and does not wedge
  the sink for the process lifetime.
- A test drives it — a handle that accepts the open and fails the write, which no
  existing test does.

* BACKLOG TASK-0PAN0 Pin the write-time rejection of retired arch_ refs at the API layer
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-0PAN0
:PRIORITY: P3
:END:

** Description

Two test gaps found by the TASK-RQ270.3.2.1 review, both NON-BLOCKING and neither
gating the excision. Filed together because they guard the same invariant.

** Gap 1 — the write-time rejection is untested at the API layer

=reject_unresolved_reference_token= is what stops a retired =arch_= id becoming
legal to ADD. There is *no test at any layer* asserting that rejection through a
real handler: =identity_lint.rs:632= tests the helper in isolation only, which is
exactly what the round's brief flagged as insufficient.

The reviewer verified the boundary holds today by code path — all four handlers
(=create_graph_heading=, =mutate_graph_heading=, =post_org_node_edit=,
=post_task_create=) call the guard under =if !req.force= at =api.rs:12971=,
=:13142=, =:13786=, =:14853=. But by code path is not by test.

*Wanted*: one api-layer test asserting a POST with =RELATES_TO=arch_GONE99= and
no =force= returns 400 through a real handler.

** Gap 2 — the invariant that actually holds the boundary is pinned by a comment

The real invariant is not "=unresolved_reference_tokens= is prefix-agnostic". It
is *"=arch_= never enters =graph.nodes=" — and that is true only because
=looks_like_structured_node_id= (=index.rs:1109=) KEEPS =arch_= in its list*, so a
=:PRODUCES: arch_X= target is not materialised as an artifact node.

Failure scenario, and it is a plausible one: after stage D someone drops =arch_=
from that list as cosmetic cleanup of a retired class. A task with
=:PRODUCES: arch_X= then materialises =arch_X= as an artifact node, it enters
=known_reference_ids=, and =reject_unresolved_reference_token= *silently stops
firing on all four write handlers*. Nothing fails. The guard just goes quiet.

*Wanted*: a test pinning =looks_like_structured_node_id("arch_X") == true=, with
the rationale as its docstring so the next reader sees why the entry is
load-bearing rather than vestigial.

*This one is carried into stage D's brief*, because stage D is what makes that
list entry the sole remaining protection.

** Gap 3 — the over-carve guard covers 3 of 5 id classes

=index.rs:2857= asserts unresolved =dec_=, =TASK-= and =term_= markers still
error. Verified real: widening the predicate to =contains('_')= or
=starts_with(\"arch\")= breaks it. It does not cover =ART-=
(=NodeIdClass::Artifact=). Low value; noted for completeness.

** Not in scope

The =is_retired_architecture_id= comment scope question (finding 2 of that
review) is *already resolved*: the manager ruled the carve-out stays
unconditional and corrected the comment in =604efd7=.

** Description
Source: vscode-orsl manager letter 2026-08-22 (operator-forwarded, 40 dispatches over 4 days, orgasmic 0.0.18). Item 2. Measured on the live daemon: 253 open fds / 256 soft limit, 223 session .jsonl handles held, 3 live runs. Root cause: writer.rs `session_handles` only evicted on LeaseSessions/shutdown.
** Shipped (commit 8bd8287)
- writer drops the handle on the `release` lifecycle append; `WriterStatus.open_session_handles` gauge + regression test.
- daemon raises RLIMIT_NOFILE at start (65536/10240/4096 fallback), logged at boot.
- `/status` carries `open_fds`/`fd_limit`; `orgasmic daemon status` prints `fds: N/limit (writer session handles: H)`.
** Leftover (d)
The exhausted daemon could not accept the health probe socket, so the supervisor logged `incumbent is not healthy … Refusing to start a competing daemon` and the sick daemon stayed up. Either answer health before the spawn path can starve it, or treat a held lock whose owner cannot answer health as dead.

* BACKLOG TASK-2B215 hermes records no NativeRuntime, so its transcripts are neither resumable nor attributable    :drivers:hermes:sessions:evidence:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-2B215
:PRIORITY: P2
:RELATES_TO: dec_Y5MPK TASK-VB9DQ TASK-H0TYV TASK-SGRTX TASK-F9VEZ TASK-B6D8W
:END:

Filed by TASK-H0TYV (VB9DQ fix round) from the recorded cross-harness matrix. Sibling of TASK-F9VEZ (codex) and TASK-B6D8W (cursor-agent).

`HermesAdapter` never overrides `HarnessEventAdapter::native_runtime`, so it takes the trait default `None` (`crates/orgasmic-drivers/src/trait.rs:248`).

The session id is server-minted and post-launch: `sessionId` is read out of the `session/new` result in `on_ws_thread_started` (`crates/orgasmic-drivers/src/adapters/hermes.rs:287-292`, method name at `:327`) and surfaced only inside `Ready.capabilities`. As with cursor-agent, ACP gives no slot for a client-supplied session id.

Consequences: no `resume_native_fork` for hermes runs, and dec_Y5MPK item 6 attribution is not computable — 82 JSONL files under `~/.hermes/sessions` on the operator machine (measured 2026-07-28), none attributable to an orgasmic dispatch. The absolute number is small; the property is the same.

The transcript finder already resolves `~/.hermes/sessions/<id>.jsonl` from the Ready `session_id` at **high** confidence, and notes the paired `session_<id>.json` is metadata only (`crates/orgasmic-drivers/src/transcript_finder.rs`). Emitting NativeRuntime turns that into a recorded path rather than a recomputed one.

Work: emit `NativeRuntimeMeta` from the `session/new` result — provider `hermes`, session id, `~/.hermes/sessions/<id>.jsonl`, and a resume argv verified against the binary. Hermes is the cheapest of the three to prove because its path rule is the simplest.

Blocked on the same contract decision as its siblings, recorded against TASK-SGRTX.

* BACKLOG TASK-37WN7 serve announces readiness before it installs the SIGTERM handler, so the announcement is not a precondition for signal delivery    :test:cli:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-37WN7
:PRIORITY: P3
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/orgasmic-cli/**,verify/flake-registry.toml
:END:

** Description
=sigterm_exits_through_graceful_shutdown_rather_than_default_disposition=
(=crates/orgasmic-cli/tests/daemon_lifecycle.rs:319=) failed once under
parallel load during TASK-YN5FJ.1 and passed everywhere else.

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH A TASK RATHER THAN A SHRUG: the test ALREADY carries a
mitigation for exactly this race. =wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= was added by
TASK-Q07Y5 precisely because =serve= registers its SIGTERM handler AFTER
=Daemon::run= returns, so a SIGTERM sent on the strength of a successful connect
can land on the default disposition. Its own comment says the window is
"invisible on an idle machine" but not "under a loaded test binary".

So this is not an unmitigated race — it is a mitigation that does not hold. Either
=wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= does not actually prove the handler is
installed, or there is a second window it does not cover. That distinction is the
task.

** Evidence
Measured 2026-08-05 during TASK-YN5FJ.1, on =bb2fb24=:
- implementer full =scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-cli=: 1 failure, this test;
- same test rerun in isolation by the wrapper: PASS;
- whole =daemon_lifecycle= binary alone: 6 passed / 0 failed;
- second full =run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-cli=: GREEN;
- manager own gate run on the merged tree: GREEN, this test did not fail.

The change under test touched =dispatch-close= argument handling only and cannot
reach =orgasmic serve=, so it is not a regression from that work.

UPDATE 2026-08-05, and it CORRECTS this task own framing.

The panic this task asked someone to capture arrived on its own, as the sole REAL
failure of the =scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-cli= gate on the TASK-M47E5.2
merge (=b20fba5=). The failing assertion is =status.signal()= — the process really
did die on SIGTERM default disposition — NOT the 30s =try_wait= deadline. So the
handler genuinely was not installed when the signal landed, which is exactly the
window =wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= claims to close.

THE LOAD-ONLY READING IS WRONG. This task, and the TASK-Q07Y5 comment it quotes,
both say the window is "invisible on an idle machine". Measured immediately after
the failure, alone, against the already-built binary: 1 failure in the first 14
isolated runs, then 12/12 green. So it reproduces WITHOUT load at roughly 7%. The
"passes in isolation" folklore — which the wrapper own isolation retry reinforces
every time it goes green — has been hiding a defect that is not load-dependent at
all. Anyone measuring this by running it once in isolation will conclude wrongly.

REGISTERED, now that the bar this task set is met: =898c7e3= adds a
signature-bearing entry owned by this task, pinned to the =status.signal()=
assertion only, so a failure on the deadline branch or the exit-code branch still
reads REAL. The first acceptance item ("the failing assertion is identified from a
captured red, not inferred") is DONE. What remains is the second: strengthen
=wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= so the window is genuinely closed, or record why
it is not worth closing.

** Why it is NOT in verify/flake-registry.toml yet
Deliberate, and this is the part to not undo casually. No panic signature was
captured — the failure was observed through the wrapper verdict, not a saved log.
A registry entry with no =signature= makes EVERY future failure of that test name
read as this known flake, which is precisely the "trains everyone to discount
failures" failure the registry exists to prevent. Registering it blind would buy
a quieter suite at the cost of the signal.

So: capture the panic first (which assertion — the =status.signal()= one, or the
30s =try_wait= deadline), THEN either fix the mitigation or register the entry
with that signature and this task as owner.

** Acceptance
- The failing assertion is identified from a captured red, not inferred.
- Either =wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= is strengthened so the window is
  genuinely closed under load, or a signature-bearing =[[flake]]= entry is added
  with this task as owner and a rationale for why the race is not worth closing.
- =scripts/run-tests.sh --check= stays green (owner must be an open task).
** Mechanism found — the mitigation watches the wrong side of the boundary
**The mechanism is now known, and it retires the "either/or" this task was filed
with.** Manager traced it 2026-08-05 against =f60af0a=. Do not re-derive it.

=serve= (=crates/orgasmic-cli/src/main.rs=) does this, in this order:

: :2299   let _ = writeln!(io::stdout(), "  press Ctrl+C to stop");
: :2300   wait_for_shutdown_signal().await;
: :2320       match signal(SignalKind::terminate()) {   // <- handler installed HERE

And =wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= (=daemon_lifecycle.rs:29=) waits for
exactly that =press Ctrl+C to stop= line on stdout.

So the helper proves the process reached a point *strictly before* registration.
It observes the WRONG SIDE OF THE BOUNDARY. This is not a mitigation that fails
under load — it is a mitigation that is STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of closing the
window it was built for, and no amount of strengthening the helper can fix it,
because the thing it would need to observe has not happened yet when the only
observable signal is emitted.

That also explains the measurement better than the load hypothesis did: the race
reproduces at roughly 7% with NO load at all (1 failure in the first 14 isolated
runs, then 12/12 green). Load was never the variable. The window is simply always
there, and 7% is how often a SIGTERM sent immediately after the print lands
inside it.

=== This changes the acceptance

The task as filed offered a legitimate terminal outcome: "register the flake with
a rationale for why the race is not worth closing". *That branch is now
withdrawn.* Its premise was that closing the race might be expensive or subtle.
It is neither — the fix is to install the SIGTERM handler BEFORE announcing
readiness, so that the announcement means what every caller already assumes it
means.

=== Is it a real defect or only a test artifact? Real, but narrow.

In ordinary operation a SIGTERM arrives long after startup and cannot land in a
microsecond window. The exposure is the restart path: =launchctl kickstart -k=
sends SIGTERM, and a KeepAlive-thrashing daemon can be signalled promptly after
boot (see the =orgasmic-local-update-launchd= history). When it does land there,
the consequence is the one TASK-WGXKD.1 built the graceful shutdown to prevent:
no release-finalization drain, no writer shutdown.

So: worth fixing, not worth panicking about. P3 is the right priority.

=== Corrected acceptance

- =serve= installs its SIGTERM handler BEFORE it prints =press Ctrl+C to stop=,
  so the readiness announcement is a true precondition for signal delivery.
- SIGINT gets the same treatment or an explicit note saying why not —
  =tokio::signal::ctrl_c()= has its own registration point with the same shape,
  and leaving one of the two half-fixed is how this returns.
- The existing test passes without =wait_until_serve_awaits_signals= needing to
  become cleverer; if the helper survives, it is because it is still a useful
  readiness gate, not because it is load-bearing for this race.
- The =verify/flake-registry.toml= entry owned by this task is REMOVED in the
  same change — the excuse expires with the defect. =scripts/run-tests.sh --check=
  stays green.
- An injection proof is appropriate and the defect is pinnable: pre-fix, the
  reordering is absent and the pinned red is the =serve died on SIGTERM's default
  disposition= assertion. Note the difficulty honestly — at ~7% a naive replay is
  not deterministic, so the proof needs to force the window (a test hook that
  delays registration) rather than hope for it.

* BACKLOG TASK-3HR8R A task parked in in_review with no reviewer dispatch is invisible
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3HR8R
:PRIORITY: P2
:END:

** Description

A task can sit in =in_review= forever with no reviewer dispatch and nothing
surfaces it. Hit live: TASK-M47E5.1 merged at [2026-08-05 Wed 18:09:04], landed
=in_review=, and no reviewer was ever dispatched. It was found hours later by an
ad-hoc board census, not by any tool.

** Why the existing controls all miss it

- =dispatch-status= lists OPEN dispatches. The failure is the ABSENCE of one, so
  the verb is structurally blind to it.
- The handoff's own hygiene rule is "a task in =in_progress= with no dispatch is
  claiming work nobody is doing". =in_review= with no dispatch is the same defect
  wearing a healthier-looking stage, and the rule as written does not cover it.
- Nothing else reads lifecycle stage against dispatch history at all.

The stage is the problem: =in_progress= with no worker LOOKS wrong to a human
skimming a board, and =in_review= looks like patience.

** Two independent sources, which is why this is filed rather than deferred

1. TASK-4WKNX's reviewer suggested exactly this as a follow-up — "a
   =dispatch-status= diagnostic for a =FIX_SUBTASK= parked =in_review= with no
   reviewer dispatch would make the intended trade harder to miss". The manager
   deferred it as usability polish on a workflow that now works.
2. The M47E5.1 miss, found independently the same day, shows it is not polish.
   The =FIX_SUBTASK= case the reviewer named is one instance; the general case
   costs a review that the active goal requires.

The reviewer reasoned forward from a design change and the sweep reasoned
backward from a real miss, and they landed on the same gap. That agreement is
the argument for building it.

** Design notes, not a design

- The signal is cheap and already on disk: the last =implementer.done= for a task
  versus any later =manager.dispatch_started= of kind =reviewer= for it. No new
  state.
- =dispatch-status= is the natural home — it is what a manager already runs — but
  it currently answers "what is open", so adding "what is stalled" widens its
  contract. Decide that deliberately rather than by accretion.
- Beware making it fire on a task that is legitimately parked. A stall needs an
  age threshold or an explicit "awaiting" marker, or it becomes noise a manager
  learns to skim past, which is how the current blindspot got here.
- The =FIX_SUBTASK= case is now the COMMON case, not an edge one: since
  TASK-4WKNX every fix round lands =in_review= by default.

** Acceptance

- A task in =in_review= whose last implementer close has no subsequent reviewer
  dispatch is surfaced by a verb a manager already runs.
- Reconstructing the TASK-M47E5.1 situation surfaces it.
- A task legitimately awaiting a reviewer dispatched moments ago does NOT
  surface.

* BACKLOG TASK-3J1YB NativeRuntimeMeta.credential_mode agrees across the recovery-claim round trip by coincidence of matching None literals
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3J1YB
:PRIORITY: P3
:END:

From TASK-QRTT8's audit (2026-07-29): Lifecycle::NativeRuntime has no credential_mode field (session.rs:422-431), so recovery_claim.rs:1730 and :2043 hard-code None when rebuilding NativeRuntimeMeta from a session, and api.rs:8303 hard-codes the same None into planned_native_runtime. The two sides of the claim-verification != agree BY COINCIDENCE of matching literals, with no test pinning that they must. If either side ever starts carrying the real mode (the claude adapter already writes Some into the meta at launch), claim verification silently starts rejecting valid claims. Ask: either persist the mode in Lifecycle::NativeRuntime so both sides carry the truth, or pin the current both-None normalization with a test naming the invariant and a comment at each literal pointing at the other. Small; the value is that the coincidence stops being silent.

* BACKLOG TASK-3R3EZ Quarantine missing project/worktree records, warn once, and add project remove    :daemon:project:recovery:
:PROPERTIES:
:DEPENDS_ON: TASK-FZB6T
:ID: TASK-3R3EZ
:PRIORITY: P2
:END:

Fix the repeated missing `ddd/.orgasmic/project.org` warning at its actual source: run-inventory polling revalidates historical RunMeta worktrees and logs on every request. Also complete board lifecycle so an operator can intentionally deregister a project.

Behavior:
1. The run catalog stores worktree/project authority as verified, missing, invalid, or unavailable with the observation time and file identity. Missing/pruned worktrees for pid-gone terminal history become stable tombstoned metadata and are not attach candidates. Inventory reads do not touch or warn about the same missing path repeatedly.
2. A registered project whose root or `.orgasmic/project.org` disappears transitions to `unavailable`; emit one structured warning/event per transition, retain last-good read state where safe, stop project refresh/repo-url/session scans, and unwatch paths that still have a watch. Reappearance triggers revalidation and a recovery event. Do not silently deregister on one ENOENT because removable volumes and temporary renames are valid.
3. Add `orgasmic project remove <id>` through the daemon writer. It removes only the board registration/watch/index entry, never the repository or its `.orgasmic` files. Default output previews the target identity/path; support idempotency and require an explicit confirmation or force flag in noninteractive use. Refuse when live runs/leases still belong to the project unless an explicit safe cleanup flow resolves them first.
4. Board refresh must diff added and removed entries: start watches/load added projects, unwatch/drop removed projects, and never leave stale index entries.

Regression: poll `/api/runs` repeatedly with several records pointing at one pruned worktree and assert zero repeated filesystem reads/warnings after the first classification; remove a board project and assert its watch/index vanish while files remain; simulate temporary disappearance/reappearance and assert one unavailable and one recovered event. Measure warning volume, not only return values.

* BACKLOG TASK-3RTM0 spawn_detached's stdout target and the drifted meaning of dropped_log_writes    :daemon:ops:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3RTM0
:PRIORITY: P3
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/**
:END:

** READ THIS FIRST — STATUS
Filed from the TASK-G64ZH.1.1 review, F-4 and F-5, both LOW and non-blocking. The
review's full text for these two was LOST to the defect described in TASK-QGWK7
(=dispatch-close= deletes the worker report), so what survives is the finding
TITLES plus their anchors, recovered from the close tx. A worker should re-derive
the detail from the code — both are small and the anchors are exact.

** F-4 — =spawn_detached= points process stdout at the durable path itself
=crates/orgasmic-cli/src/daemon_lifecycle.rs= (the detached fallback, ~=:435-461=).
PRE-EXISTING SHAPE, not introduced by the G64ZH chain. The detached spawn
redirects the child's stdout at the same durable log the daemon opens, which is
the original TASK-ZBYH3 shape — two writers on one inode — surviving in the one
launch path that is not a service definition. The reviewer noted the tail case
involves =spawn_detached= after =keep= rotations.

Note this path is now mirror-suppressed via =ORGASMIC_LOG_MIRROR=off= (TASK-G64ZH.1),
so the daemon's own tracing does not double-write; what remains is where stray
=println!=/panic output goes, which is exactly what the service definitions were
changed to send to =daemon.stdout.log= instead.

** F-5 — =dropped_log_writes= now counts PRESERVED lines, and =--no-log-mirror='s help text has an undocumented exception
Two small consequences of TASK-G64ZH.1.1's write-time fallback:
- The counter's meaning drifted. The G64ZH chain settled it as "one per line that
  never landed in the durable file", but a line that falls back to stdout is
  PRESERVED, not lost — so the counter now conflates "lost" with "written
  somewhere else". Decide the meaning and document it, or split the two.
- =serve --no-log-mirror='s help text says the mirror is suppressed, without the
  exception that it is now restored whenever the durable handle is missing. The
  flag no longer means "never write to stdout". Correct the text.

** Acceptance
- =spawn_detached='s stdout target is a deliberate choice with a stated reason,
  not an inherited default — either changed to match the service definitions or
  documented as intentionally different.
- =dropped_log_writes= has ONE documented meaning, and if the fallback should not
  count toward it, it does not.
- =--no-log-mirror='s help states the durable-handle exception.

* BACKLOG TASK-3TQ0R Extend the driver-resolution fence to daemon integration tests
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3TQ0R
:IMPLEMENTS: TASK-3NJ9K
:PRIORITY: P2
:TEST_CMD: cargo test -p orgasmic-daemon
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/orgasmic-daemon/**
:END:

** Description

TASK-3NJ9K routed daemon driver resolution through =crate::driver_resolution=
and fenced it under =cfg(test)=: =resolve_driver= default-denies harness-exec
modes, and =resolve_launch_driver= additionally refuses a mux address whose
harness that mode would exec.

=cfg(test)= is enabled only while compiling the lib's own test harness. An
integration test in =crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/= links the lib built
*without* it, so both functions there are the production pass-through. The
entire fence — default-deny, the panic, the launch seam — is absent for that
whole body of tests.

This is not hypothetical reach. =tests/dispatch_preflight.rs= boots a real
daemon and =POST=s =/dispatch= with ={"mode": "acp-stdio", "harness":
"claude"}=, i.e. the ordinary dispatch surface with a provider address, over
HTTP. Others carry provider harnesses too: =tests/integration.rs=
(=acp-stdio=/=codex=), =tests/dispatch_credential_plan.rs=,
=tests/recovery_fault_restart.rs= (=tmux=/=claude= session fixtures driving boot
reattach).

Audited 2026-07-30: those dispatches are refused before any spawn, because each
test engineers an unusable credential and asserts the 400. That is genuinely
host-independent — =classify_bare_api_key= refuses an empty key without reading
the Keychain — so **no integration test is known to spawn a provider today**.

The defect is structural, not a live leak: the safety is a property each test
supplies for itself, exactly the shape of the ="unreachable without a hermes
binary"= comment that caused the original incident. Nothing stops the next
integration test from posting the same address without engineering a refusal,
and the fence that exists to catch precisely that cannot see it.

** Acceptance

- A daemon integration test that resolves or launches a real harness-exec
  address is refused the same way a lib unit test is, with the same named,
  host-independent message pointing at the stub.
- The mechanism cannot be =cfg(test)=. Options to weigh and decide in writing:
  a runtime test-profile flag the daemon sets when booted by
  =Daemon::run(.., test_options())=; a cargo feature the =[dev-dependencies]=
  self-dependency enables; or moving the launch seam behind a trait the test
  harness substitutes. Whichever is chosen must not be settable in a production
  build.
- Production behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged, and the guard costs nothing
  in a release build.
- The existing integration coverage keeps working: the preflight tests must
  still reach their 400 refusals, and the recovery/reattach tests must still
  resolve mux drivers for sessions they created themselves.
- A regression test proves the guard from inside =tests/=: an integration test
  that asks for =acp-stdio=/=claude= is refused, on any host, with and without
  the provider binary installed.
- Audit every file under =crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/= for provider
  addresses; migrate those whose address is incidental to the stub, and list in
  the worklog the ones that legitimately need a real address and why.

** Prior Evidence

TASK-3NJ9K fence: =crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/driver_resolution.rs=, merged
=75fe95f=. Launch-seam gap found in manager review and closed in =32c3f8c=.
Original incident: =tx-20260730-orgasmic-3992=. Integration reach:
=crates/orgasmic-daemon/tests/dispatch_preflight.rs= around line 200.

* BACKLOG TASK-3ZR2E driver_modes tests race on the process-global ORGASMIC_DRIVER_SIMULATE
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3ZR2E
:PRIORITY: P3
:END:

** Description

=adapter_fixtures_cover_public_harness_event_shapes= fails in the parallel
=driver_modes= test binary and passes the isolation rerun. Found by the
TASK-M47E5.1 reviewer, which also identified the mechanism rather than reporting
a shrug.

*Mechanism*: the test mutates the PROCESS-GLOBAL env var
=ORGASMIC_DRIVER_SIMULATE= (=crates/orgasmic-drivers/tests/driver_modes.rs:1646=)
while =installed_harnesses_answer_their_own_readiness_probe= REMOVES it in the
same binary (=:2152=). Cargo runs tests in one process across threads, so the two
race. Both predate TASK-M47E5.1 and neither reviewed file participates.

** This is a test-isolation defect, not a flake to wave through

The registry exists for failures the project is willing to see and not act on.
This one has a known, cheap, local cause: two tests sharing mutable process
state. Registering it would buy a quieter suite at the cost of the signal, and
the fix is smaller than the excuse.

*Deliberately NOT registered in =verify/flake-registry.toml=*, and for the same
reason TASK-37WN7 was initially left out: NO PANIC SIGNATURE WAS CAPTURED. The
reviewer reported the test name and the runner's verdict, not the assertion text.
A signature-less entry makes every future failure of this name read as this known
race, which is exactly the "trains everyone to discount failures" outcome the
registry exists to prevent.

Note the registry behaved correctly here: the unregistered failure was reported
REAL, which is what surfaced it at all.

** Acceptance

- The two tests no longer share mutable process-global state — serialize them, or
  scope the variable to the spawned child rather than the test process.
- Prefer the child-scoped fix if the production code allows it: a test-only
  serialization lock is a constraint future tests must remember, which is the
  same class of maintenance dependency as an enumeration list.
- =scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-drivers= is green in the PARALLEL run, not
  only in isolation.
- If it is registered instead, capture the panic first and pin the signature.

* BACKLOG TASK-45F0N acp_ws.rs breaks its select without draining the socket — same shape as SVKPN's fixed defect, different lifecycle
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-45F0N
:PRIORITY: P3
:END:

From TASK-SVKPN's driver audit (2026-07-29): acp_ws.rs:277 (commands / ws.next() select) breaks on channel close and on release-done without draining the socket — the same break-without-drain shape SVKPN fixed in subprocess_stream_json and acp_stdio. Deliberately NOT fixed there: no child process, no SubprocessExitSummary, no empty-run_complete synthesis (the product harm SVKPN was about), and the release path closes the socket first — a fix would drain a just-closed socket on an unmeasured path. The loss, if any, is transcript events only. Measure before fixing: construct a fast-closing ws peer and check whether produced frames are lost; if yes, apply the SVKPN bounded-drain pattern (RELEASE_DRAIN_BUDGET derivation, drain after close-initiation, biased select inside the drain); if no, record the negative result and close.

* BACKLOG TASK-48SFW Any orgasmic verb run against a staged ORGASMIC_HOME restarts the real daemon and kills every live dispatch    :dispatch:daemon:runtime:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-48SFW
:PRIORITY: P1
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/orgasmic-cli/**, crates/orgasmic-daemon/**
:END:

SECOND HYPOTHESIS, and it implicates the MANAGER rather than the workers. Added
before the evidence is in, so the record is not shaped by which answer turns out
to be more comfortable.

Both incidents happened while a manager MONITOR was polling =orgasmic status= and
=orgasmic manager dispatch-status= every 90 seconds. There is a documented
behaviour — the memory =orgasmic-runtime-reinstall=, and =install.sh='s trailing
=orgasmic status= — that =orgasmic status= AUTO-SPAWNS a daemon when it does not
find a reachable one. An auto-spawn writes the LaunchAgent, and that would
produce exactly the measured signature: plist mtime equal to the restart instant,
no shutdown lines in the log, and =launchctl runs = 1= because the job was freshly
loaded rather than restarted by KeepAlive.

Under this reading the causal chain inverts. Something makes the daemon briefly
unreachable — a slow request, a drain, load — the polling =status= call misses it,
auto-spawns, and the spawn restarts the daemon and kills every live run. The
workers are victims rather than the cause, and the manager's own monitoring is
the trigger.

THE TWO HYPOTHESES ARE DISTINGUISHABLE, AND THE EXPERIMENT IS RUNNING. As of
=00:16Z= no workers are dispatched, and a watcher samples boot_id and plist mtime
every 75 seconds — polling =orgasmic status= at the same cadence that was live
during both incidents, with the workers removed.

- Daemon restarts during that watch => the workers are exonerated and the polling
  path, or something else ambient, is the trigger.
- Daemon stays stable across a window longer than the ~9 minute incident interval
  => polling alone is not sufficient, and the worker hypothesis stands.

WHICHEVER WAY IT LANDS, ONE FIX IS COMMON TO BOTH and should be built regardless:
no routine, read-only status call should ever be able to start a daemon as a side
effect. A read that mutates the LaunchAgent is a trap for every caller, not only
this one, and it is the same defect shape as the =install.sh= trailing-status
trap already recorded in the runtime-reinstall memory.
EXPERIMENT RESULT [2026-08-03 00:26Z] — the second hypothesis is REFUTED as a
sole cause, and the first stands.

Ten consecutive minutes of stability, =03:16:33= to =03:26:33= local, sampling
=boot_id= and the LaunchAgent plist mtime every 75 seconds with NO workers
dispatched. Every sample identical: boot =2f2fcd57=, plist mtime =1785715985=.

That watch polled =orgasmic status= at essentially the cadence that was live
during both incidents (90s then, 75s here) and ran LONGER than the ~9 minute
interval between them. So polling =orgasmic status= does not, by itself, restart
the daemon. The managers monitoring is exonerated as a sole cause.

What survives: A DISPATCHED WORKER IS A NECESSARY INGREDIENT. That is consistent
with the primary hypothesis — a worker invoking a daemon lifecycle verb, which
rewrites the one real LaunchAgent regardless of =ORGASMIC_HOME= — and it is now
the only reading still standing.

Not yet distinguished, and worth naming rather than glossing: whether the trigger
is the WORKERS OWN command, or something the daemon does on the dispatch path
(spawning a mux, writing a run record) that briefly makes it unreachable to a
concurrent caller which then spawns. The next dispatch is deliberately a
READ-ONLY reviewer carrying an explicit prohibition on daemon lifecycle verbs and
no render-check instruction at all: if it survives, the worker-command reading is
supported; if it dies, the dispatch PATH is implicated rather than anything the
worker chose to run.

Still worth building either way, unchanged: a routine read-only status call must
never be able to start a daemon as a side effect.
DISCRIMINATOR RESULT [2026-08-03 00:4xZ] — THE WORKER-COMMAND READING IS
SUPPORTED, and the dispatch path is exonerated.

The next dispatch after the experiment was deliberately built to separate the two
survivors: ONE worker, read-only reviewer, no render-check instruction, carrying
an explicit prohibition on every daemon lifecycle verb.

IT COMPLETED NORMALLY. Full review delivered, =dispatch finalize= called, and the
LaunchAgent-mtime watch fired no rewrite event for its entire run. Its own report
states: "No daemon start/stop/restart/serve command, no launchctl, and no
forbidden billed test was run."

So a dispatch does NOT restart the daemon by existing. Something a worker CHOSE
to run did. Combined with the earlier ten-minute polling watch, both alternative
explanations are now eliminated:

| hypothesis | verdict | evidence |
|------------+---------+----------|
| manager polling =orgasmic status= auto-spawns | REFUTED as sole cause | 10 min stable, no workers, same cadence |
| the dispatch PATH restarts the daemon | REFUTED | lone read-only worker completed untouched |
| a worker INVOKES a lifecycle verb | STANDS | only reading left; prohibition worked |

WHAT THIS MEANS OPERATIONALLY, and it should go in every brief until the code
fix lands: the prohibition is currently the only thing standing between a
concurrent dispatch fleet and a total loss. It worked on first use. It is also
one sentence in a brief that a worker under momentum can skip, which is exactly
the argument for the refusal being enforced in the CLI rather than requested in
prose — the same reasoning TASK-3CM0Q makes about tier declarations.

MANAGERS OWN CONTRIBUTION, restated now that the cause is known: the briefs
that told workers to "stage an ORGASMIC_HOME from the edited files" were the
likely invitation. That instruction is still CORRECT and still necessary — the
live daemon serves installed content, not the worktree — but it must always
travel with the prohibition and with the safe recipe (run the worktrees own
=target/debug/orgasmic entry= against the staged home; never start a daemon).
ROOT CAUSE, FOUND IN SOURCE [2026-08-03 01:53Z]. Everything above this line was
inference; this is the code path, and it corrects the earlier guidance.

: ensure_running(home)                       daemon_lifecycle.rs:152
:   -> ensure_running_local(home, _)                          :159
:     -> start_via_selected_adapter(home)                     :419
:       -> daemon_service::start(home) => ServiceStart::Persistent

On macOS the persistent adapter WRITES AND LOADS
=~/Library/LaunchAgents/orgasmic.daemon.plist=. That path is PER-USER. It is not
scoped by =ORGASMIC_HOME=, and nothing in the call chain notices that the home it
was handed is not the home the LaunchAgent already serves.

So the rule is much wider than "do not run daemon lifecycle verbs":

*ANY =orgasmic= VERB THAT NEEDS A DAEMON, RUN AGAINST A STAGED =ORGASMIC_HOME=,
RESTARTS THE REAL DAEMON.* The staged home has no daemon listening, so
=ensure_running= fires, the adapter rewrites the one real plist to point at the
staged home, launchd reloads it, and every live run on the machine dies. The
worker does not have to type =daemon start=. It only has to run a normal command
with a different home.

THE EVIDENCE THAT ISOLATED IT. TASK-VEGRV was live in ALL THREE outages and
absent from both dispatches that survived. It died 4-6 minutes in each time, and
its pane capture before the first one reads: "All four gates are passing. Now I
need to test the render output by staging the edited files into a temporary
ORGASMIC_HOME and running the entry command." The concurrency theory does not
survive the data either — four concurrent workers ran from 23:09 to 23:46 with no
outage.

THE MANAGER CAUSED THIS THREE TIMES. The render check was a manager instruction,
in a manager-authored brief, and the "safe" rewrite after the second outage was
also a manager instruction — it still ran an =orgasmic= verb against a staged
home, so it was not safe at all. The prohibition added after outage two forbade
lifecycle verbs and therefore did not cover the actual trigger. Two dispatches
survived it and I read that as the prohibition working; they survived because
they had no render check.

CORRECTED GUIDANCE, until the code refuses:
- NEVER set =ORGASMIC_HOME= to anything other than the ambient one inside a
  dispatch, for ANY =orgasmic= invocation.
- A shipped-content change does NOT need a render check to be verified. The
  parse is covered by =cargo test -p orgasmic-core --test fixtures=
  (=parses_shipped_schema_files=), the verb and flag claims by
  =cargo test -p orgasmic-cli --test cli_parity=, and the injection point by
  reading =inject_default_workflow=. Ask for those instead.
- If a rendered artifact genuinely must be inspected, it has to be produced
  without invoking the CLI against a foreign home — read the shipped files
  directly, or add a unit test that exercises the injector in-process.

THE FIX THIS IMPLIES IS BIGGER THAN THE ORIGINAL TASK. =ensure_running= should
refuse, or at minimum warn loudly, when the home it is asked to start differs
from the home the installed LaunchAgent already serves. A per-user service
mutated as a side effect of a per-home read is a trap for every caller, and the
=install.sh= trailing-status trap already recorded in the runtime-reinstall
memory is the same defect wearing a different hat.
THE SAFE PATTERN, found by the TASK-3CM0Q worker and CONFIRMED BY MEASUREMENT
[2026-08-03]. This is what every test and probe that needs a real daemon should
have been doing all along.

Set =ORGASMIC_DAEMON_URL= on the CHILD process. =ensure_running= returns before
=start_via_selected_adapter= is ever reached, so no adapter starts, no
LaunchAgent is written, and the operator daemon is never touched. The existing
=crates/orgasmic-cli/tests/manager_register.rs= already relies on this; it was
simply never written down as the rule.

=crates/orgasmic-cli/tests/manager_tier_cli.rs= spawns the built binary against a
real booted daemon and walks a full undeclared-read -> declare -> read-back ->
refuse -> re-declare sequence. The manager ran it and then checked
=~/Library/LaunchAgents/orgasmic.daemon.plist=: mtime UNCHANGED. So the pattern
is verified, not merely argued.

Contrast with what the three outages did: stage an =ORGASMIC_HOME= and invoke a
verb, which has nothing listening, so =ensure_running= proceeds to the adapter
and rewrites the one real per-user plist.

*The rule to write into briefs and tests from now on:*
- need a real daemon in a test => point the CHILD at one with
  =ORGASMIC_DAEMON_URL=;
- never stage =ORGASMIC_HOME= to get isolation, because it does not isolate the
  LaunchAgent;
- =env -u ORGASMIC_HOME= to strip a LEAKED value is the opposite of staging one
  and remains correct.

This also sharpens the code fix this task asks for. =ensure_running= already has
a cheap correct path when it is told where the daemon is; the defect is that
absent that, it silently escalates to mutating a per-user service. Refusing —
or at minimum warning — when the home it is asked to start differs from the one
the installed LaunchAgent serves would have turned all three outages into an
error message.
RULE SHARPENED BY MEASUREMENT [2026-08-03]. The blanket "never set
=ORGASMIC_HOME=" is the right thing to put in a brief, but it is not the precise
rule, and the code fix should be built against the precise one.

Measured: =ORGASMIC_HOME=<staged> orgasmic doctor= with residue staged in the
fake home printed the expected warning AND left the LaunchAgent plist mtime
unchanged (=04:53:32=, from hours earlier) with the daemons boot_id and pid
untouched. So =doctor= genuinely does not reach =ensure_running=.

The precise rule is therefore *never set =ORGASMIC_HOME= for a verb that NEEDS
THE DAEMON* — because that is what triggers =ensure_running= ->
=start_via_selected_adapter= -> the per-user LaunchAgent write. Read-only local
verbs that never open a connection are unaffected.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, and they point in opposite directions on purpose:

1. *Keep the blanket ban in briefs.* A worker cannot reliably know which verbs
   open a daemon connection, the failure is total and silent when it guesses
   wrong, and the cost of the blanket version is nearly zero because the
   daemon-free verification recipe covers what workers actually need. Precision
   here would buy nothing and risk everything.
2. *Build the code fix against the precise rule.* =ensure_running= is the single
   choke point and already has a cheap correct path when it is told where the
   daemon is (=ORGASMIC_DAEMON_URL=). Refusing — or warning — when the home it is
   asked to start differs from the one the installed LaunchAgent serves would fix
   the class without touching verbs like =doctor= that are already safe.

That asymmetry is the useful part: the guidance humans and agents read should be
blunter than the invariant the code enforces.

** Description

INFERENCE, LABELLED AS SUCH — the evidence is strong and circumstantial, and no
worker artifact survived to prove it directly.

Two dispatch-wide losses on 2026-08-03, ten minutes apart:

| time (UTC) | killed | transport |
|------------+--------+-----------|
| 00:03-00:04 | TASK-VEGRV, TASK-3CM0Q, TASK-FZB6T reviewer | rmux |
| 00:13:05    | TASK-VEGRV, TASK-FZB6T reviewer            | tmux |

The second event rules out the transport as the cause: it happened on tmux, after
the manager switched away from rmux precisely because rmux had died in the first.

WHAT IS MEASURED
- =~/Library/LaunchAgents/orgasmic.daemon.plist= has mtime *03:13:05 local*,
  which is exactly the =00:13:05Z= daemon restart instant. The first event shows
  the same pattern, with TWO boot_ids logged one after the other at =00:04:11Z=
  (a plist reload race).
- The daemon logged NO shutdown lines before either restart. It goes straight
  from steady-state to =starting pre-bind boot work=, so it was killed hard.
- =launchctl print gui/501/orgasmic.daemon= reports =runs = 1= and
  =last exit code = (never exited)=, so this is NOT launchd KeepAlive restarting
  a crashed process.
- No orgasmic crash report exists for 2026-08-03 (latest is 2026-07-31). Memory
  was 61% free with zero swap, so it is not an OOM kill.
- The plist still points at =~/.orgasmic/bin/orgasmic=, so the BINARY was not
  hijacked — only the plist was rewritten and reloaded.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. Something rewrote the LaunchAgent plist, twice, at the exact
instants the daemon restarted. The memory =orgasmic-daemon-start-hijacks-launchagent=
and the existing gotcha both record that =orgasmic daemon start= rewrites THE ONE
REAL LAUNCHAGENT PLIST regardless of =ORGASMIC_HOME= — a per-user path, not a
per-home one. A worker running any daemon lifecycle verb therefore restarts the
operator daemon and kills every sibling dispatch, including itself.

THE MANAGER CONTRIBUTED TO THIS. Several briefs this session instructed workers
to "stage an =ORGASMIC_HOME= from the edited files" for a render check, because
the live daemon serves INSTALLED shipped content rather than the worktree. That
instruction is correct and necessary, and it is one short step from
=orgasmic daemon start= against the staged home — which is not isolated at all.
The instruction was given without the accompanying prohibition.

** Why this is P1

It makes concurrent dispatch unsafe outright. Five workers died in ten minutes,
three with live uncommitted work that had to be salvaged by hand. Nothing warns
the worker, nothing warns the manager, and the failure looks like a transport
problem — the manager initially and wrongly blamed rmux, switched transports, and
lost the next two workers the same way.

** Work

- A daemon lifecycle verb invoked from inside a dispatch (=ORGASMIC_RUN_ID= is
  set in the worker environment) should REFUSE by name, and say why: it would
  restart the operator daemon and kill every live run including your own.
- Consider whether =ORGASMIC_HOME= should scope the LaunchAgent path at all, or
  whether the honest answer is that daemon lifecycle is never per-home and the
  verb should say so.
- Give workers a SAFE render path that needs no daemon: the 2026-08-03
  TASK-0JY7M worker did it correctly by running the worktrees own
  =target/debug/orgasmic entry= against a staged home. Document that as the
  supported recipe so the dangerous one is not reinvented.
- Until this lands, every dispatch brief must carry an explicit prohibition.

** Acceptance

- A daemon lifecycle verb from inside a dispatch refuses, with a message naming
  the consequence.
- The supported no-daemon render recipe is documented where brief authors will
  find it.
- A regression proves the refusal fires when the dispatch environment is present
  and does not fire for an ordinary operator invocation.

* BACKLOG TASK-4DTBZ rmux review transport must survive auth-shadow and daemon disconnects    :drivers:rmux:claude:hardening:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4DTBZ
:PRIORITY: P1
:RELATES_TO: TASK-QSX56
:END:

Two consecutive TASK-QSX56 reviewer dispatches blocked the required Opus verdict for different transport reasons. Attempt 1 inherited a stale ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN from the foreground daemon and native Claude returned 401 even though the stored claude.ai login was healthy. After restarting the daemon with provider auth overrides removed, attempt 2 reached real Claude Opus 4.8/high and performed substantive analysis, then the rmux daemon closed the pane-output-cursor transport after 4m25s; the worker released protocol_end_without_finalize and no report was preserved. Define explicit provider-auth environment precedence/scrubbing for rmux launches, and make a daemon-side rmux disconnect preserve or reattach the native Claude session/report rather than losing the review. Add deterministic regressions for stale auth shadowing and rmux daemon disconnect during an active reviewer session.
HARD EVIDENCE [2026-08-03], and it is worse than "survive auth-shadow and daemon
disconnects": THE RMUX DAEMON DIED UNDER THREE CONCURRENT DISPATCHES AND KILLED
ALL OF THEM AT ONCE.

Measured. At =2026-08-03T00:03:10Z= the orgasmic daemon logged, for all three
live runs within 24 milliseconds:

: ERROR supervisor: driver release failed; continuing unconditional producer and
:       lifecycle cleanup  run_id="run-...a0f17bb2..." / "...f6cae37c..." / "...a642ea86..."
: (hint: verify the rmux daemon is running and the endpoint is reachable) and CLI
:  fallback (driver transport unavailable: rmux send child exited with exit status: 1)
: WARN api: dispatch completion watcher: release without worker finalize, flagging orphan  x3

Then the orgasmic daemon restarted at =00:04:11Z= — TWICE, two different boot_ids
one after the other, which is the launchd KeepAlive race. No machine reboot:
uptime was continuous at 7h01m and no new panic reports exist. =rmux ls= returned
EMPTY afterwards while a NEW =rmux-daemon= pid was already up.

Casualties: TASK-VEGRV and TASK-3CM0Q implementers, both with uncommitted work
(preserved by the manager as =ad368c6= and =a409197=), and the TASK-FZB6T round-3
reviewer, which lost its entire run. Three workers, one transport failure.

RMUX CYCLED ITS PID AT LEAST THREE TIMES during the 2026-08-02/03 session
(=6049= at 20:06, =99375= later, =3150= after this incident), so this is not a
one-off. It leaves NO trace: =rmux.err.log= has not been written since
2026-07-26, and there is no crash report in either DiagnosticReports directory.

WHY THIS IS SHARPER THAN ITS PRIORITY SUGGESTS. rmux was chosen for every
dispatch that session precisely BECAUSE it is the only pane transport with a
liveness channel in the installed runtime (=57e35de= predates TASK-4CSMYs tmux
channel). So the safe-looking choice is the one that lost three workers, and the
alternative — tmux — is only unsafe because the runtime has not been rebuilt.
Whichever way a manager turns today, one of the two failure modes is live.

WHAT A FIX HAS TO COVER, beyond the original scope:
- rmux dying must not be silent. It currently writes nothing anywhere.
- a driver-release failure across MULTIPLE runs at once should be recognisable as
  a transport-level event rather than reported three times as unrelated run
  failures.
- the orphan flagging is correct but the recovery is not: three workers with live
  work were left with no route to finalize, and the manager had to salvage two
  worktrees by hand.
- consider whether the daemon should refuse to keep dispatching onto a transport
  whose endpoint it has just failed to reach.

* BACKLOG TASK-4PPPE serve announces readiness before it can handle SIGTERM, so the graceful-shutdown test races itself
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4PPPE
:PRIORITY: P2
:TAGS: cli,lifecycle,flake
:END:
** Description
Found by the TASK-JQARS worker while classifying its own gate failures, and
correctly excluded from that task's scope. It is a **test defect, not a
production defect** — the production path was probed directly and is sound.

=== Measured

`crates/orgasmic-cli/tests/daemon_lifecycle.rs`,
`sigterm_exits_through_graceful_shutdown...`.

- On the JQARS branch: **3 pass / 6 runs**.
- On the pristine baseline (`git stash -u`, same command): **2 pass / 3 runs**.

It fails on both, so it is pre-existing and unrelated to that change.

=== Mechanism

The test sends SIGTERM the instant `serve` prints "press Ctrl+C to stop".
`main.rs` prints that line **before** `wait_for_shutdown_signal()` registers the
handler, so a SIGTERM that arrives inside that window hits the default
disposition and kills the process instead of running the graceful path. The
test's own comment describes the window.

Direct probe of the built binary using the test's exact home, config and
process-group setup: `rc=0` in **3/3 with SIGTERM at 0 ms delay**, and **3/3
with a 300 ms delay**. The production sequence is fine; the test races its own
readiness signal.

=== Why it matters beyond the flake

The readiness line is a **lie about readiness** for one specific consumer: a
supervisor that treats "press Ctrl+C to stop" as "safe to signal" has the same
race. Nothing in the product does that today, but the plist and any future
service adapter are exactly the kind of consumer that would. Decide whether the
line should move after handler registration, or whether a separate, explicit
readiness signal is owed — and record which, because "the test is racy" and
"the readiness announcement precedes readiness" are different bugs with the same
symptom.

=== Ask

1. Make the readiness announcement follow handler registration, or introduce a
   readiness signal that does, and say which you chose and why.
2. Remove the race from the test rather than papering it with a sleep — a sleep
   restores green without restoring the guarantee.
3. Check the same ordering question for Ctrl+C and for the service-stop path
   ATAXN's marker protocol now depends on.

=== Acceptance

- The test passes 10/10 consecutive runs, and a run with SIGTERM at 0 ms delay
  still exits through graceful shutdown.
- Prove it by injection: restore the announcement to its current position, watch
  the test fail, move it back, watch it pass — with output.
- State whether any shipped consumer (plist, installer, docs) tells an operator
  or supervisor to signal on that line.

=== Non-goals

- Do not change the shutdown budgets or the ATAXN marker protocol.

* BACKLOG TASK-52NJS a provider content filter blocks cross-family review of parser, deletion and permission code — the class where independent review is worth most    :dispatch:review:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-52NJS
:PRIORITY: P2
:END:

** Description
*MEASURED THREE TIMES ON 2026-08-08, COSTING THREE FULL REVIEW BUDGETS.* Every
codex/gpt-5.6-sol dispatch of the TASK-RMA18.1.1 review died identically: an
OpenAI content filter refused mid-turn ("This content can't be shown ... We take
extra caution with cybersecurity requests ... Trusted Access"), *the turn ENDED*,
codex returned to its idle input placeholder at 0.0% CPU, and orgasmic's stall
detector killed the run at 600s with =last.txt= 0 bytes.

*THE THIRD DEATH IS THE INFORMATIVE ONE.* The first two followed a web search
(=site:github.com/git/git read-cache.c verify_hdr index checksum hashfile=), so
the manager removed the search from the brief and pointed the reviewer at the
local =git= binary as an executable oracle instead. *The third dispatch was
refused with NO web search at all* — the pane shows the refusal landing after
purely local work: reading =manager.rs=, =dispatch.rs=, =cli_parity.rs= and a
prior review document.

So the trigger is not the search. *It is the subject matter plus the review's own
adversarial framing.* The manager's brief said the parser was "attack surface",
called its input "attacker-influenceable", instructed "Attack it", asked the
reviewer to "construct an index that parses successfully but yields the wrong
path set", and asked whether a pathname resolution was "exploitable". Combined
with the actual subject — a hand-written binary parser for git's index, symlink
handling via =openat(O_NOFOLLOW)=, and a recursive delete path — that reads as
offensive-security tasking.

*IT IS NOT. The work is the exact opposite:* verifying that a data-loss guard
FAILS CLOSED so a directory git refuses to remove is never deleted. The
adversarial vocabulary was a manager stylistic choice for rigour, and it made an
accurate description of defensive work look like something else.

** What was done about it
The brief was recast in terms that describe the work accurately — "does the
parser derive an incomplete path set from a real index git accepts", "confirm
anything it cannot fully account for is a refusal rather than a short list" —
with the substance unchanged and nothing hidden. *The round was then dispatched
same-family (claude) with the reason stated on the dispatch*, because three
failures is enough evidence that a fourth cross-family attempt is not worth
45 more minutes with the board stalled behind it.

Whether the reframing alone would have satisfied the filter is UNTESTED. It is
one hypothesis; the subject matter alone may be sufficient to trigger it.

** Why this matters beyond one round
1. *IT SILENTLY REVOKES THE CROSS-FAMILY REVIEW POLICY FOR A WHOLE CLASS OF
   WORK* — and that class is disproportionately the safety-critical kind:
   parsers, deletion paths, permission checks, credential handling. Precisely
   where an independent reviewer is worth the most, the independent reviewer
   cannot participate.
2. *IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A HANG* without the pane. See [[TASK-8VBXR]] —
   the first death was permanently unknowable; the second and third were
   diagnosed in one read each from an external snapshotter the manager had armed
   in the meantime.
3. *IT IS DETERMINISTIC.* Same brief, same investigative path, same refusal. A
   manager who re-dispatches without changing the brief burns the budget again,
   which is exactly what happened between deaths one and two.

** Recommended
1. *Record the constraint where dispatch decisions are made*, so a manager
   choosing a reviewer for a parser/deletion/permission task knows cross-family
   may not be available and budgets for it. Already added to =gotchas.org=.
2. *Write briefs in the register the work actually occupies.* Defensive work
   described defensively is both more accurate and more portable across
   harnesses. Adversarial phrasing bought no rigour that "does this fail closed,
   and what input makes it fail open" does not.
3. *Consider a pre-dispatch dry-run probe* for cross-family reviews of this
   class — one cheap turn that asks the harness to restate the assignment. A
   refusal there costs a minute rather than a budget. Speculative; not measured.
4. If a stall-kill's pane shows a provider refusal, orgasmic should classify it
   as such rather than as "no work evidence" — [[TASK-8VBXR]] acceptance item 5.

** Evidence
Preserved pane frames:
- =.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/task-rma18-1-1-review/pane-at-stall-kill-run-20260808T124951.txt=
  (death 2, refusal after the web search)
- =.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/task-rma18-1-1-review/pane-at-stall-kill-run-20260808T130710.txt=
  (death 3, refusal with NO web search — the decisive one)
Aborted dispatches: =tx-20260808-orgasmic-5361=, =-5372=, =-5393=.

* BACKLOG TASK-5M45A Hermes ignores the provider and model a dispatch asks for    :P1:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-5M45A
:END:

Measured 2026-07-25 on hermes 0.16.0, driving `hermes acp` directly with the
same JSON-RPC handshake `acp_stdio` performs.

On the hermes stdio path orgasmic transmits the dispatch's provider and model
only inside `thread_start._meta.orgasmic` (`spawn_payload`, hermes.rs), and the
argv is a bare `hermes acp`. Hermes does not read them. Two `session/new`
calls, identical but for the provider:

  provider = "anthropic"             -> currentModelId ollama-cloud:glm-5.2
  provider = "nonexistent-provider"  -> currentModelId ollama-cloud:glm-5.2

Neither errored. Both landed on hermes's own configured default. An unknown
provider id is not even rejected, so there is no signal that the request was
dropped.

Consequences, in order of how much they cost:
1. A dispatch that specifies a provider silently runs on a different one. The
   operator is billed to the wrong account and gets a different model's output,
   with nothing in the session to say so.
2. It is worse than invisible, it is actively misreported: the `Ready` event's
   capabilities echo `cfg.provider` and `cfg.model` back
   (`on_ws_thread_started`), so the session JSONL records the provider that was
   ASKED FOR as though it were the one in use. Reading the session is the normal
   way to find out what a run did, and here it lies.
3. It blocks a hermes readiness probe. Checking a credential requires knowing
   which credential the launch consumes; while the provider is ignored, orgasmic
   cannot know. See the comment on `HermesAdapter` (TASK-TJKFC decided against a
   probe on exactly this ground).

Not yet established: whether hermes exposes any supported way to select a
provider per ACP session (a `session/set_config_option` equivalent, an argv
flag, or an env var). The adapter already builds a `/model ... --provider ...`
slash command in `transition_state`, so mid-run switching works; whether that
same path can be driven at startup was not tested. The fix might be as small as
issuing that command once after `session/new`.

Minimum acceptable outcome if selection turns out to be impossible: stop echoing
a provider and model the run is not using, so the session records what actually
happened rather than what was requested.

* BACKLOG TASK-5NJR4 Bounded boot reattach declines a truncated file whose live acquire sits in the unread gap — decide the recovery
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-5NJR4
:PRIORITY: P3
:END:

From TASK-7QM8M (2026-07-29), the deliberate rule-1 boundary: a truncated session file whose newest retained segment does not own the file's end yields NO candidate — including the shape where the live run's own Acquire/RunMeta sit in the unread middle. The whole-file read would have reattached it. Only legacy residue files can have that shape today (manager_launch_ids gives external/terminal launches their own files), and the run stays visible as recoverable through the inventory path. Options 7QM8M named: a larger tail window for manager-shaped files, or a bounded backwards seek for the newest Acquire when rule 1 fails. Decide with a constructed legacy-shaped fixture; do not widen silently.
