** Description

During TASK-95SGV.2 a daemon test (commit =560eb77=, probed on main as
=f215bb7=) called =spawn_worker_run= with a real =StageWorker { driver:
"acp-stdio", harness: "hermes" }=. The author guarded the second call
(after the injected refusal was released) with the assumption that the branch
is *unreachable without a hermes binary*. On CI that holds; on a developer
machine =hermes= is on =$PATH=, so every test execution spawned a real
=hermes acp= subprocess and a billed ollama-cloud turn. The spawned agents
outlived the test (run release does not reap the subprocess), became PPID-1
orphans, mutated main, and re-ran the test — each run spawning another copy
until the hermetic rewrite =184813f= merged as =b510b30= (spawn window
07:22–07:35, 12+ real agent sessions).

The class of defect: nothing in the daemon prevents a test from resolving a
*real* driver/harness. Host-dependent assumptions convert into provider spawns
silently.

** Acceptance

- In the daemon's test profile (=cfg(test)= and/or an explicit test-mode flag
  the API fixtures set), driver/harness resolution must refuse to construct
  any transport that can exec a real subprocess harness: only the stub driver
  (and any purpose-built in-process fakes) are resolvable.
- The refusal is loud: resolving =acp-stdio=, =rmux=, or any future real
  driver under the test profile fails the test with an error naming the
  driver and pointing at the stub, rather than silently substituting.
- Production resolution paths are byte-for-byte unaffected; no runtime check
  is added outside the test profile without justification.
- A regression test proves the guard: a test that requests a real driver via
  the ordinary dispatch surface must get the refusal, on any host, with and
  without a =hermes= binary on =$PATH=.
- Audit the existing daemon test suite for other =StageWorker= constructions
  naming real drivers/harnesses and migrate them to the stub; list the
  migrated sites in the worklog.
- No test in the suite may depend on the presence *or* absence of a
  provider binary on the host.

exactly; orphan env traced to the fix2 correction session; orphan prompts were
the fixture task title verbatim. Unsafe construction: =560eb77=
=crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/api.rs= lines ~21926 and ~22010. Hermetic rewrite:
=184813f=, merged =b510b30=. Dispatch closed with containment record
=tx-20260730-orgasmic-3992= (properties CONTAINMENT/ORPHAN_PGIDS/FORENSICS).

* DONE TASK-3X5AQ Dispatch worktree builds prompt for Documents and leave dead TCC rows — chosen shared-target-dir fix is measurably unsound, needs a new decision :dispatch:runtime:macos:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-3X5AQ
:PRIORITY: P1
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/orgasmic-daemon/**, crates/orgasmic-cli/**, shipped/**
:END:

=== READ THIS FIRST — STATUS ===
The DECISION recorded below (option 2, shared =CARGO_TARGET_DIR=) was DISPROVED
by measurement later the same day. DO NOT IMPLEMENT IT. See the section
"Disproof of the shared target dir (2026-08-03)" at the end of this task: a
shared target dir makes a worker's =cargo build= a silent no-op and greens its
integration suite against another checkout's binary. This task needs a NEW
decision; option 5 (stable worktree slots) is the recommendation.
=== END STATUS ===

DECISION [2026-08-03]: take option 2, the shared =CARGO_TARGET_DIR=. The
operator chose it after the cost of option 1 was measured (it disables the whole
orgasmic-cli integration suite, including the =cli_parity= false-verb guard).

CONCURRENCY IS HANDLED BY CARGO, PROVEN NOT ASSUMED. Two =cargo build= runs
against one target dir were started 2s apart; the second printed:

: Blocking waiting for file lock on artifact directory
: Finished `dev` profile ... in 0.13s

So workers need no coordination protocol and cannot corrupt each other — the
second simply waits. That answers the "how does a worker know" question: it does
not have to.

THREE THINGS THE LOCK DOES NOT COVER, and they are the real design work:

1. *The lock covers BUILDING, not TESTING.* Once artifacts exist, =cargo test=
   just runs binaries, and two workers can run suites concurrently against the
   same target dir with no lock at all. That is exactly the load condition
   measured FIVE times this session to redden the live-mux and process-probe
   tests spuriously. A shared target dir does not cause that, but it removes the
   incidental staggering that per-worktree builds provided.

2. *Flag divergence causes rebuild thrashing.* =cargo clippy --all-targets=,
   =cargo test -p orgasmic-daemon --lib= and =cargo build --release= select
   different artifact sets; workers alternating between them invalidate each
   other and each waits for a rebuild of what the other just discarded. With a
   25 GB target and multi-minute daemon builds this is the dominant cost, and it
   is worse than the lock wait. MITIGATION: briefs should name ONE gate command
   set and workers should not improvise flags — largely already true, and now
   load-bearing rather than stylistic.

3. *Shared blast radius.* One worker running =cargo clean=, or a disk-pressure
   cleanup, destroys every concurrent workers artifacts mid-run. Worth an
   explicit "never cargo clean in a dispatch" line alongside the other
   prohibitions.

ONE CLEAR WIN, measured: each worktree currently carries its own target —
=task-8ed6v= alone is 3.0 GB against the shared 25 GB. Sharing removes that
duplication per concurrent worker, which also reduces the =syspolicyd= scan
surface, since the gotcha attributes the bursts to executing freshly written
binaries.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: the daemon composes the worker environment, so
=CARGO_TARGET_DIR= belongs there rather than in a per-brief instruction — a
prose instruction is skippable and this needs to hold for every dispatch. Point
it at the repo-root =target/=, which already holds the TCC grant; that is what
makes the prompts stop.

macOS TCC keys Documents-folder access by BINARY PATH. Every dispatch worktree
lives at a fresh path under
=~/Documents/code/tools/orgasmic/.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/<task>/worktree/=, so a
worker that builds =target/debug/orgasmic= there produces a program macOS has
never seen. It prompts the operator, and the grant it earns dies with the
worktree.

*Measured 2026-08-03.* The user TCC db has five
=kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDocumentsFolder= rows under =dispatch/*/worktree=, and
ALL FIVE point at worktrees that no longer exist:

: .../dispatch/task-vegrv/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    granted 03:41:23, worktree GONE
: .../dispatch/task-2dftx/worktree/target/release/orgasmic  GONE
: .../dispatch/task-CZTWD/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE
: .../dispatch/task-Y2ZQJ/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE
: .../dispatch/task-jj9rd/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE

So the prompt is not a grant that failed to stick. It is a NEW grant request per
dispatch, for a path created and destroyed within the hour, and approving it does
nothing for the next worker.

*NOT the runtime reinstall.* Checked at the same time and stated here because the
coincidence is misleading: =~/.orgasmic/bin/orgasmic= holds
=kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles= = 2, last modified 2026-08-02 18:35:46 — BEFORE
the 2026-08-03 reinstall — with zero permission errors and all 6 projects
indexed. The codesign preserved TCC exactly as intended.

** Description

macOS TCC keys Documents-folder access by BINARY PATH. Every dispatch worktree
lives at a fresh path under
=~/Documents/code/tools/orgasmic/.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/<task>/worktree/=, so a
worker that builds =target/debug/orgasmic= there produces a program macOS has
never seen. It prompts the operator, and the grant it earns dies with the
worktree.

*Measured 2026-08-03.* The user TCC db has five
=kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDocumentsFolder= rows under =dispatch/*/worktree=, and
ALL FIVE point at worktrees that no longer exist:

: .../dispatch/task-vegrv/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    granted 03:41:23, worktree GONE
: .../dispatch/task-2dftx/worktree/target/release/orgasmic  GONE
: .../dispatch/task-CZTWD/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE
: .../dispatch/task-Y2ZQJ/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE
: .../dispatch/task-jj9rd/worktree/target/debug/orgasmic    GONE

So the prompt is not a grant that failed to stick. It is a NEW grant request per
dispatch, for a path created and destroyed within the hour, and approving it does
nothing for the next worker.

*NOT the runtime reinstall.* Checked at the same time and stated here because the
coincidence is misleading: =~/.orgasmic/bin/orgasmic= holds
=kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAllFiles= = 2, last modified 2026-08-02 18:35:46 — BEFORE
the 2026-08-03 reinstall — with zero permission errors and all 6 projects
indexed. The codesign preserved TCC exactly as intended.

** Why it has not broken anything yet

A worker denied Documents access still reaches =.orgasmic/= state through the
daemon over HTTP, so no run has failed on this. The costs are operator
interruption, a TCC db slowly filling with dead paths, and the risk that an
operator conditioned to dismiss orgasmic prompts dismisses one that matters.

** Same family as TASK-48SFW

Per-user OS state that per-dispatch isolation does not scope. There it was the
LaunchAgent plist; here it is the TCC path grant. Worth fixing with that in mind
rather than as a one-off.

** Options, and the trade is real

1. *Tell workers never to build the CLI.* Simplest, and the operator asked for
   this first. COST, measured: =cargo test -p orgasmic-cli= builds the binary
   automatically for integration tests (=CARGO_BIN_EXE_orgasmic=), so this
   disables essentially the whole CLI integration suite —
   =cli_parity= (the TASK-TKR0H false-verb guard, load-bearing for every shipped
   prose change), =entry=, =doctor=, =status=, =reindex=, =list_output=,
   =node_body_roundtrip_cli=, =task_property_silent_drop_cli=, =bootstrap_smoke=,
   =pinned_exec=, =manager_tier_cli=, =manager_register=. Several of those caught
   real defects in the 2026-08-02/03 session.
2. *Shared =CARGO_TARGET_DIR=.* Point worktree builds at one stable path that
   already holds the grant. Every test keeps working and no new prompt is ever
   raised. Cost: concurrent workers serialize on the cargo lock, and a shared
   target dir is a known contention source.
3. *Move dispatch worktrees outside =~/Documents=.* Removes the whole class —
   Documents is the only guarded ancestor — but changes a path a lot of tooling
   and several gotchas assume, and the daemons own Documents grant exists
   precisely because the project lives there.
4. *Prompt-free by construction:* have the dispatch env set =CARGO_TARGET_DIR=
   only for the CLI crate, or have workers run the INSTALLED
   =~/.orgasmic/bin/orgasmic= (already granted) for anything that just needs a
   working CLI rather than the one they are changing.

Options 2 and 4 keep the suite; 1 and 3 change what workers can verify. Pick
deliberately.

** Acceptance

- A dispatch that builds and runs the CLI raises no new Documents prompt.
- Whatever is chosen, the CLI integration suite still runs for a worker that is
  CHANGING the CLI — that is the case where the tests matter most.
- Existing dead worktree rows in the TCC db are documented as safe to remove (it
  is SIP-protected, so removal is operator-only through Settings).
** Disproof of the shared target dir (2026-08-03)
STOP — THE 2026-08-03 DECISION IS DISPROVED. Do NOT implement the shared
=CARGO_TARGET_DIR=. It is not merely contended, it is UNSOUND: a dispatch
worker's =cargo build= becomes a silent no-op and its integration suite greens
against a DIFFERENT checkout's binary.

*Reproduced 2026-08-03 in the exact production shape* — a git worktree of a
cargo workspace, both pointed at the repo-root target dir (cargo 1.94.1):

: repo root:        main.rs prints MAIN_BRANCH   -> cargo build -> target/debug/probe-cli = MAIN_BRANCH
: git worktree A:   main.rs prints TASK_A_BRANCH -> cargo build -> "Fresh probe-cli", NO compile
:                   target/debug/probe-cli still = MAIN_BRANCH
:                   cargo test in worktree A: 1 passed, BIN_SAYS=MAIN_BRANCH

The worker edited a source file, built, and tested. Nothing errored. The suite
was green. It ran the MANAGER's binary.

*Mechanism, and why the earlier lock measurement missed it.* The file lock is
real and does serialize concurrent builds — that measurement was correct and is
not what fails. What fails is freshness. Cargo's =-C metadata= hash for a path
package does not include the checkout path, so BOTH checkouts share ONE
fingerprint directory (=target/debug/.fingerprint/probe-cli-<hash>=, verified: a
single dir, not one per worktree). Freshness is then decided by comparing the
mtimes of the files recorded in the OTHER checkout's dep-info. The worker's own
edited file is not in that list, so nothing looks stale and cargo reports
=Fresh=. The stale uplifted binary at =target/<profile>/<name>= is what
=CARGO_BIN_EXE_*= resolves to, so every integration test inherits it.

It is also NOT ordering-dependent: after making worktree B's file genuinely
dirty and rebuilding, rebuilding worktree A reported =Fresh= and left B's binary
in place. Either checkout can silently receive the other's program.

*Why this outweighs the problem it was chosen to solve.* The TCC prompt costs
the operator a click and leaves a dead db row; no run has ever failed on it.
This trades that for a class of false green — and this session already lost real
work to two of those (a re-cut =orgasmic verify= artifact that never reached its
assertions, and a shipped artifact that became a false green when a fix made its
defect unreproducible). The whole point of the gate is that green means
something. Sharing a target dir across checkouts makes green mean nothing, in a
way no test on this repo would detect.

*Option 5, which satisfies BOTH constraints — the recommendation.* The tension
is: TCC needs the EXECUTED BINARY PATH to be stable across dispatches, while
cargo needs ONE checkout path per target dir. A fixed pool of stable worktree
slots gives both:

: .orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/slot-1/worktree  (own target/)
: .orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/slot-2/worktree  (own target/)   ... N slots

A slot's binary path never changes, so the operator grants it ONCE and the grant
survives — the prompt stops for good and the TCC db stops filling with dead
rows. Each slot keeps its own target dir with exactly one checkout path in it,
so cargo's freshness logic is the ordinary, sound, single-checkout case. Two
concurrent workers never share a slot, so there is no lock contention and no
flag thrashing either. Disk is bounded at N targets instead of unbounded, which
is strictly better than today.

Cost: the dispatch directory is named by slot rather than by task, so the
task->worktree mapping has to be read from the dispatch record instead of the
path. Several gotchas and briefs name task-shaped worktree paths and would need
updating, and slot release has to be part of worktree teardown.

*Reopened for a decision.* The operator picked option 2 on 2026-08-03 with the
lock measurement in hand and without this one; that choice should not be
executed as recorded. Options 1 and 3 stand as previously described. Option 5 is
the recommendation.
** The cdhash measurement: option 5 withdrawn, and the general-vs-specific split
OPTION 5 (STABLE WORKTREE SLOTS) IS WITHDRAWN AS THE TCC FIX. The manager
recommended it on 2026-08-03 on the assumption that a STABLE BINARY PATH keeps a
TCC grant. Measured 2026-08-05: it does not. The premise was wrong.

*The measurement.* Decoding the =csreq= blob stored on each grant in the user
TCC db:

: worktree-built binary   -> cdhash H"b081c98ab06c6ab3611c357bdb900420b3e66d54"
: installed runtime binary -> identifier "com.theaspirational.orgasmic" and
:                            certificate root = H"a70531007cd128ff081597cb27bee0816613d86d"

A grant for a linker/ad-hoc-signed binary is pinned to that binary's exact
CONTENT HASH, not to its path. Rebuild the same file at the same path and the
cdhash changes, so the grant no longer matches and macOS prompts again.

*Consequence, and it inverts the recommendation.* Slots would make the prompt
fire ONCE PER BUILD instead of once per dispatch — strictly WORSE than today,
since a worker builds many times per dispatch. Any scheme whose mechanism is "a
stable path earns a durable grant" fails for the same reason.

*What actually makes a grant durable* is the second row: a stable SIGNING
IDENTITY. =identifier ... and certificate root= survives rebuilds, which is
exactly why the 2026-08-03 runtime reinstall kept its Documents access while
the gotcha warns that a linker-signed binary is "a stranger to TCC". That is a
real fix but not one orgasmic can apply generally — it cannot codesign arbitrary
projects' build outputs, and requiring a signing identity to run a dispatch is a
much heavier ask than the problem justifies.

=== The remaining general fix is option 3, and the framework owns it
Get dispatch worktrees OUT of TCC-guarded directories, rather than trying to
make grants survive. macOS guards =~/Documents=, =~/Desktop=, =~/Downloads= and
iCloud Drive; nothing outside them needs a grant at all, so there is no cdhash
to invalidate and no prompt to answer.

This is the right layer because ORGASMIC CREATES THE PROBLEM: it chooses to put
worktrees at =<project>/.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/<task>/worktree=, which inherits
whatever guarded ancestor the project root has. A project rooted in
=~/Documents= gets it for free and cannot opt out.

*To verify before building* (do not assume, this task has already burned one
assumption): a worktree outside Documents still has a =.git= file pointing at
=<project>/.git/worktrees/<name>= INSIDE Documents. Confirm whether git
operations from the worker trip a prompt, and if so whether a separate git dir
or a shared clone avoids it.

=== Is this orgasmic-specific or general? — general, with a specific accent
GENERAL: any orgasmic project that (a) runs on macOS, (b) COMPILES BINARIES it
then executes, and (c) is rooted under a guarded folder. Interpreted projects
mostly escape it because the executed binary is the interpreter
(=/usr/bin/python3=, =node=), which is already known to TCC; it is freshly
COMPILED output that is a stranger. So Rust, Go, C/C++, CGo, Tauri and Electron
projects hit it; plain Python/Node/Ruby ones typically do not.

SPECIFIC to this repo: only the vocabulary of the disproved fix
(=CARGO_TARGET_DIR=) and the fact that this project happens to live in
=~/Documents=. Neither belongs in the framework.

=== So: bundle the behaviour, do not write a convention
- The FIX belongs in the daemon's worktree placement — one code path, applies to
  every dispatch in every project, nothing to remember.
- A repo-wide convention is the wrong instrument for the reason already recorded
  here ("a prose instruction is skippable and this needs to hold for every
  dispatch") and for a reason this session demonstrated three times: prohibitions
  in prose get missed. The ORGASMIC_HOME outages happened WITH a written
  prohibition in force.
- Do NOT bundle toolchain knowledge. Orgasmic should not know what cargo is. If
  a per-project environment is ever needed, it should be a generic
  project-declared env map, not a =CARGO_TARGET_DIR= special case.

=== What slots are still worth
Bounded disk (N targets instead of one per concurrent worktree, measured at
3.0 GB for a single worktree) and, if anyone ever revisits sharing a target dir,
they are the only shape that keeps cargo sound. Keep them on the table as a
disk/scale change; just not as the TCC answer.
** Verification and recommended placement (2026-08-05)
VERIFIED 2026-08-05, before building anything. Four measurements, one of which
closes the option-5 question for good and one of which corrects an earlier
assumption in this task.

1. *A rebuild at a STABLE PATH changes the cdhash.* Built a tiny ad-hoc-signed
   binary twice at one path:

   : build 1: CDHash=16237ab166c90df05f15b3f29b0f25c03d7616c9
   : build 2: CDHash=6cdc20d7c7e6574d879e6b72648f0c1922a79120

   The TCC grant is pinned to the cdhash, so it cannot survive a rebuild. Option
   5 (stable worktree slots) is CONFIRMED DEAD as the TCC fix — it would move
   the prompt from once-per-dispatch to once-per-BUILD.

2. *git is NOT exempt, but it is already satisfied and path-stable.* Earlier
   reasoning here assumed git would be covered as an Apple binary. Wrong:
   =/opt/homebrew/Cellar/git/2.52.0_1/bin/git= holds its own
   =kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDocumentsFolder= grant, as do =tmux= and =rustup=.
   They prompted once historically and stuck, because their paths are stable.
   Crucially, across the FIVE recorded dispatch prompts, every grant was for a
   freshly built =.../worktree/target/{debug,release}/orgasmic= — NEVER for git.
   So git reaching into a Documents-hosted =.git= was already a solved case
   during real dispatches. (A Homebrew git upgrade moves the path and re-prompts
   once; that is pre-existing and unrelated to worktree placement.)

3. *A worktree outside the repo works normally.* Created one at
   =~/.orgasmic/worktrees/orgasmic/tcc-probe=: its =.git= file resolves back to
   =<repo>/.git/worktrees/tcc-probe= inside Documents, =git status= and
   =git log= work, =.orgasmic/project.org= is present so project resolution
   still works from the worktree, and =git worktree remove= works from outside
   the repo. Same filesystem (=/dev/disk3s5=), so no cross-volume concerns.

4. *The toolchain builds and runs there.* cargo built and ran a fresh binary
   under =~/.orgasmic/worktrees/...= with no issue.

*LIMIT OF TEST 4, STATED SO NOBODY OVER-READS IT.* The probe binary also read
the Documents-hosted repo successfully and RAISED NO PROMPT — but that proves
nothing about dispatches. It ran under this shell, whose responsible process
already holds Documents access; TCC attributes to the responsible process, and a
dispatch's chain (daemon -> tmux -> harness -> cargo -> test binary) is
different. The argument for the fix does NOT rest on that result. It rests on
the fact that a worker whose worktree is outside Documents HAS NO REASON to read
Documents at all: its cwd, sources, target dir and =.orgasmic= snapshot are all
inside the worktree, and the only link back is the =.git= file, which git — a
separately granted, path-stable binary — follows.

=== Recommended placement
: ~/.orgasmic/worktrees/<project-id>/<task-id>/

Keyed on PROJECT ID, not display name: the id is what the CLI and daemon already
use everywhere (=--project <id>=), and names can collide or change.

Why a TOP-LEVEL =worktrees/= rather than the proposed
=~/.orgasmic/user/projects/<name>/worktrees=:
- =user/= currently means user-level CONFIG — it holds =auth/= and =board.org=,
  both small. Worktrees are multi-GB regenerable scratch; mixing them buries the
  largest thing on disk inside a config namespace.
- =user/= also carries a bad association: =user/workers/= was the retired
  residue that TASK-8ED6V was filed about. A new =user/projects/= invites the
  same "is this live or dead?" question that incident was about.
- Top-level makes the cost visible: =du -sh ~/.orgasmic/*= shows it at a glance.

Why NOT =~/Library/Caches/orgasmic/...=, the otherwise idiomatic macOS choice:
it is unguarded (confirmed: zero TCC rows for Cache services), but macOS may
PURGE it under disk pressure, which would destroy a worktree mid-dispatch.
Rejected on that alone.

=== What moves and what stays
Move only the SCRATCH. The dispatch RECORD — brief, report =last.txt=, stdout
log under =.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/<task>/= — stays in the project, because it is
part of the durable record, it is small, and it is written by the daemon, which
is identity-signed and already granted. Splitting on "record stays, scratch
leaves" keeps every existing brief-path reference valid.

=== Already has an escape hatch
=orgasmic manager dispatch --worktree <PATH>= already exists ("omitted -> a
managed path under =.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/="). So this change is to the MANAGED
DEFAULT only, and the override is precedent, not new surface.

=== Make it universal, not macOS-gated
Linux has no TCC, but the move is still correct there: the repo stops
accumulating multi-GB build trees, =git status= in the repo stays clean, and
disk is attributable per project. One code path beats a platform branch.

=== Known follow-on work
=.orgasmic/tmp/dispatch/<task>/worktree= is named in gotchas, briefs and
memories; those need updating with the change. =dispatch-close
--worktree-remove= must remove from the new root, and the salvage ref
=refs/orgasmic/salvage/<sha>= is git-level so it is unaffected.
** Implementation task
FILED [2026-08-05] as TASK-M47E5 — "Move dispatch worktrees out of TCC-guarded
directories, and give them a prune" (P1).

It carries both halves deliberately. Part 1 is the relocation to
=~/.orgasmic/worktrees/<project-id>/<task-id>/=. Part 2 is pruning, and it is a
REQUIREMENT of the move rather than a follow-up: today a stray worktree sits
inside the repo where =git status= and =git worktree list= surface it, so after
the move the same leak becomes SILENT multi-GB accumulation. Shipping the
relocation alone would trade visible garbage for invisible garbage.

This task (TASK-3X5AQ) stays open only as the measurement record — the cdhash
proof, the disproved shared target dir, and the disproved stable slots. The work
lives on TASK-M47E5.

* DONE TASK-4BBA6 move the syspolicyd watchdog inside run-tests.sh: the guard that stops a Mac-wide reboot lives in prose and was skipped again :testing:hardening:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4BBA6
:PRIORITY: P1
:WRITE_SCOPE: scripts/run-tests.sh,.orgasmic/gotchas.org
:VERIFIED:    scripts/run-tests-selftest.sh: 61 passed, 0 failed (2026-08-13); watchdog code and gotcha mechanism already landed in 1f8eed8
:END:

** READ THIS FIRST — STATUS
Filed [2026-08-08] immediately after the manager rebooted this machine by running
=scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-daemon= with no watchdog. Third occurrence of
the chain: =WindowServer-2026-08-08-105749.ips=, after =2026-07-29-112228= and
=2026-08-02-200136=.

** What happened
=.orgasmic/gotchas.org= carries the remedy already, and has since 2026-08-03:

: IF YOU MUST RUN THE SUITE WHILE UNATTENDED, GUARD IT. syspolicyd is pid-stable
: per boot; sample ps -o pcpu= -p <pid> every 10s and kill the cargo run if it
: holds above ~400% for a minute.

The manager READ that entry in full during bootstrap, then ran the suite without
the guard, because the sentence is conditioned on =WHILE UNATTENDED= and the
manager classified itself as attending. That classification is wrong, and the
wrongness is the point: a manager fires a command and waits for a completion
notification, so nobody is sampling the load curve — which is the only thing the
guard does. The preceding paragraph of the same entry establishes that the burst
comes from test EXECUTION, which does not care who is watching.

*So the condition does not discriminate, and a reader who applies it faithfully
still reboots the machine.* This is the project index case of a claim measured on
some situations and written down as a universal.

** Why this is not a docs fix
TASK-M47E5.3 ruled, on a different destructive path, that *a protection that
lives in a document is not a protection*. The same ruling applies here and has
now been paid for three times. Rewording the gotcha produces a fourth reader who
reasons their way around it.

The watchdog is ~10 lines of shell, and =run-tests.sh= is already the single
chokepoint every suite invocation goes through — CI (=ci.yml:191=), every
dispatched worker, and every manager. Putting it inside the script makes the
protection structural: unskippable, and applied identically by all three.

MEASURED THE SAME DAY, and it is why the guard is cheap: the full daemon lib
suite re-executed against the already-built binary on a calm host ran
*738 passed / 0 failed in 49.37s* with syspolicyd flat at 0%. The run that
rebooted the machine was the same suite through cargo under load. The guard costs
nothing on the fast path.

** Direction
1. Sample =syspolicyd= CPU from inside =run-tests.sh= for the life of the cargo
   run, on the interval and threshold the gotcha already names (~400% sustained
   for ~60s), and kill the run when it trips.
2. A trip is NOT a code verdict. It is the same class as the existing
   =INCONCLUSIVE= exit 4 — the host, not the diff — and must classify that way
   rather than as a failure. Do not let it read as green either.
3. Say what it did, loudly, in the summary: the sampled rate, the threshold, and
   that the run was truncated by the guard.
4. Only then trim the gotcha entry to point at the mechanism instead of asking
   the reader to implement it.

** Acceptance
- A =run-tests.sh= invocation that drives syspolicyd above the threshold for the
  sustained window is killed BY THE SCRIPT, with no watchdog written by the
  caller.
- The guard trip classifies as host-state (exit 4 family), never as REAL and
  never as green, and the summary names the measured rate.
- The guard is active on every path into the script, including per-crate =-p=
  runs; =--classify= runs execute nothing and are trivially inert.
- A selftest case covers the trip, in the same style as the existing ladder cases.
- =.orgasmic/gotchas.org= no longer asks the reader to build the sampler.
** Evidence
MEASURED BY A WORKER'S OWN WATCHDOG [2026-08-08], TASK-2QK4P.1's daemon gate.
This is the strongest argument yet for putting the guard inside =run-tests.sh=,
and it is not the argument the task was filed on.

The worker ran =scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-daemon= under the mandated
10s-sampling watchdog. The gate's own VERDICT said:

: host : calm (threshold syspolicyd_rate>=1.50; load=8.21 elevated (>=8.0), corroborating only)
: delta load=8.21 syspolicyd_cpu=117.8 wall_s=168
: rate  0.7012

*While the watchdog simultaneously recorded a genuine ~20-second syspolicyd burst
PEAKING AT 796.3%*, decaying to 167% and then to single digits. The hot streak
reached 2 of the 6 consecutive samples required to kill. *Only its DURATION kept
it under the guard — its amplitude was twice the 400% line.*

*THE MECHANISM: =rate= IS TOTAL CPU OVER WALL TIME, SO IT CANNOT DISTINGUISH A
SHORT VIOLENT SPIKE FROM A LONG GENTLE SIMMER — AND IT IS THE SPIKE THAT WEDGES
tccd.* Nearly all of the run's syspolicyd CPU was concentrated in ~20 seconds,
and dividing by a 168-second wall spread it into a number that reads calm. Two
instruments looked at the same 20 seconds: the instantaneous sampler saw 796.3%,
the averaged gate saw 0.7012 against a 1.50 threshold.

This is NOT an argument that TASK-STWVB's rate design was wrong. The rate answers
"was this host degraded across the run", and the round-6 review upheld the
reasoning that a verdict must not be routed through a measurement of something
else. *It is an argument that the rate cannot serve as the REBOOT guard*, because
the reboot chain (syspolicyd -> tccd -> WindowServer) is driven by sustained
INSTANTANEOUS contention, which is exactly what an average destroys.

So the guard =run-tests.sh= needs is not a stricter threshold on the number it
already computes. It is a *second, instantaneous sampler running for the duration
of the suite* — the thing every worker is currently told to hand-roll in prose,
which is what this task exists to fix. A worker hand-rolling it is why this
measurement exists at all; a worker forgetting to is why the machine rebooted on
2026-08-08.

*ONE WORD, TWO BLIND SPOTS.* TASK-K9WWM records the same =host: calm= verdict
printed while the 1m load average at the moment of failure was 13.64-15.03. The
host word is derived from syspolicyd rate and is structurally blind BOTH to a 10s
HTTP budget expiring under scheduler pressure AND to an instantaneous CPU spike.
Whatever this task ships should say plainly what the word does and does not
cover, because operators and workers alike read it as "was the host to blame".

=== WIDENED at filing (manager, 2026-07-29): the primary channel is missing too

Further measurement while scoping the tmux default switch. The gap is not only
JQ8AV's rescue channel — the PRIMARY pane-liveness channel is absent on tmux:

- =pane_activity= is emitted by =crates/orgasmic-drivers/src/modes/rmux.rs=
  and by nothing else. A grep for the event across =crates/orgasmic-drivers/src/=
  returns rmux hits only.
- =modes/tmux.rs= (4668 lines) sends =DriverEvent::Ready=,
  =TransitionState=, =ToolCall= and the fatal-error paths. There is no
  continuous pane-output event of any kind.

So on a tmux transport the stall clock sees driver events only when the worker
happens to call a tool or change state. Between those, evidence falls back to
the subtree CPU probe alone. A CPU-hot stretch (a long =cargo test= under the
pane) is still classified Working, so the common long-tool case survives. The
fatal case is the provider-bound think: low CPU, no tool calls, no pane event,
and — because JQ8AV's consult is gated on =transport == "rmux"= — no rescue
either. That is a 600s kill of a healthy worker with every channel blind.

This is why TASK-RWCRN's history matters: rmux only became safe when it grew
=pane_activity=. tmux has never had that, so it is where rmux was BEFORE the
fix, not merely missing the JQ8AV refinement.

ORDERING CONSEQUENCE. The operator has directed that tmux become the shipped
default driver, on the sound reasoning that a first-time user may have only
tmux. That makes this task a SHIP BLOCKER rather than a hardening nicety: with
the default flipped and this unfixed, the users least equipped to diagnose it
get healthy workers killed at ten minutes. Land this before the default flips;
dogfood on tmux in the meantime with
=--governance-json '{"stall_timeout_secs":3600}'= on every long-thinking
dispatch.

Work item 0, ahead of the others: give the tmux driver a coalesced
=pane_activity= equivalent to rmux's, with rmux's live tests ported
(=live_rmux_pane_publishes_pane_activity_while_it_writes= and the
newline-free-redraw variant) onto a test-owned tmux server. Only then does the
open-turn-statusline consult of items 1-3 become a refinement rather than the
sole channel.
PRODUCTION CONFIRMATION [2026-08-03], and this is what closes the loop the task
was opened for.

The runtime was rebuilt at =05e1813= and a TASK-8ED6V implementer dispatched on
*tmux* — the first tmux dispatch on a daemon that actually contains this channel.
Its session JSONL carries:

: driver_event/pane_activity   {"bytes": 10867, "seq": 3, "type": "pane_activity"}

Counted 2 events at +45s and 4 at +105s, increasing, with the run =[run-live]= and
=DRIVER=tmux=. So the channel is not merely compiled in — IT REPORTS, on the
transport it was written for, in production.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE TASK. Until this measurement, tmux dispatches on this
host had no progress signal at all, and a provider-bound think was released at the
stall budget regardless of how much work it was doing. That is what destroyed the
TASK-FZB6T.1 worker report on 2026-08-02: it committed 4,004 good lines and was
killed eight minutes later with its entire report unwritten.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE STANDING MITIGATION. The mandatory
=--governance-json {"stall_timeout_secs":3600}= on long tmux dispatches existed

** Description
TASK-JQ8AV landed a third work-evidence channel: at the stall deadline, when
subtree CPU is below the work threshold, the probe captures the pane and looks
for the TUI's open-turn statusline. A provider-bound turn is then classified
=Working= instead of being stall-killed.

That channel is gated on =target.transport == "rmux"= (supervisor.rs, in
=ProcessSubtreeCpuProbe=). On a =tmux= transport the consult never runs, so the
classification falls back to CPU alone — which is exactly the state that killed

** Description

Round-3 review of the pane evidence channel returned NEEDS FIXES — BLOCK SHIP
(=reviewer.done= tx =tx-20260802-orgasmic-4150=, finding =tx-4146=).

*THE FIX ROUND REINTRODUCED THE DEFECT IT WAS PROTECTING AGAINST.* TASK-4CSMY.1
replaced "any punctuation glyph" with the =STATUS_SPINNER_GLYPHS= allowlist to
stop a completed assistant row rescuing a wedge. That closed the false-RESCUE
hole and opened a false-KILL one, which is the direction no at-rest test can see.

*THE MEASUREMENT*, taken from the INSTALLED Anthropic Claude Code 2.1.220
binary — not from a fixture, not from a billed harness run:

: if(process.env.TERM==="xterm-ghostty")
:   return ["\xB7","✢","✳","✶","✻","✻"];
: return   ["\xB7","✢","✳","✶","✻","✽"];

So the real frame sequences are:
- normal:  =·= U+00B7, =✢= U+2722, =✳= U+2733, *=✶= U+2736*, =✻= U+273B, =✽= U+273D
- ghostty: same first five, =✻= repeated in the last slot

=STATUS_SPINNER_GLYPHS= (=supervisor.rs:5205-5214=) currently holds
=● ✽ · ∗ ✢ ✳ ✻ ◦=. Against that measurement:

- *U+2736 =✶= IS MISSING, and it is a real frame in BOTH sequences.* A
  provider-bound claude turn that freezes on that frame is REJECTED by the
  tightened classifier; subtree CPU stays below threshold, no new pane bytes
  arrive, and the supervisor stall-releases a healthy worker at the budget
  boundary. That is exactly the TASK-JQ8AV incident.
- U+2217 =∗= is present and appears in NEITHER sequence. It was labelled a
  "frame sibling" and is not one. Harmless in the false-kill direction, but it
  is an unmeasured entry in a table whose whole purpose is to be measured.

Manager independently re-ran the same extraction against the same binary and
confirms the reviewer byte for byte.

*WHY THE TESTS DID NOT CATCH IT*, which is the more important half. Both
real-pane acceptance arms hard-code a single glyph, =✽ Quantumizing…=
(=supervisor.rs:10767=, =10922=), and the unit loop at =10413-10419= only proves
that every entry ALREADY IN the table is accepted. A table that is missing an
entry passes both. The suite cannot distinguish a complete allowlist from an
incomplete one, so the next drift in claude''s frame set will land silently too.

** Acceptance

- =STATUS_SPINNER_GLYPHS= matches the measured production sequences: add U+2736;
  drop U+2217 unless a source is cited for it. Cite the extraction in a comment
  so the next reader can re-derive it rather than trust it.
- A positive control proves the classifier against U+2736 specifically, and at
  least one REAL rmux/tmux network-waiting pane paints =✶ Verb… (…)= rather than
  the single glyph both arms currently share.
- *The completeness gap is the real deliverable.* Adding one glyph fixes today;
  it does not stop the same silent failure next time claude changes its frames.
  Add something that fails when the table drifts out of step with the installed
  harness — a test that extracts the sequence from the installed binary when one
  is present and asserts the table is a superset, skipping cleanly when it is
  absent, is one shape. Another is a documented re-derivation recipe pinned next
  to the table. Choose deliberately and say why; do not silently ship only the
  one-character fix.
- The round-3 reviewer explicitly CLEARED two residuals — do not re-litigate
  them: keeping =·= is correct (the binary proves it is a real frame), and the

** Description
Battle-test F4: =glossary create --relates-to "Semantic Routing Model, Expanded Routing Graph"= (prose, not ids) was accepted at write time, then poisoned the whole index — one dangling-ref parse error per whitespace-separated word, surfaced only as an opaque global counter, root-causable only by grepping daemon logs. Reference-valued properties are validated exclusively at index time (=lint_dangling_graph_edges=, crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/index.rs:1060; =collect_dangling_reference_tokens=, orgasmic-core/src/identity_lint.rs:184); =render_graph_heading= (api.rs:7850) and =node prop set= write property values verbatim.

Fix: validate ref-valued properties (RELATES_TO, GLOSSARY_REFS, MOTIVATED_BY, DEPENDS_ON, IMPLEMENTS, PARENT — the dec_HJENQ vocabulary) at write time in graph create handlers and =node prop set=: every token must resolve against the index snapshot. Reject with an error naming the property, the offending token, and the expected format (space-separated node ids); =--force= escape hatch for intentional forward references. Document the value format in the =--relates-to= / =--property= help text. Write-time rejection costs one retry; index-time poisoning cost a debugging session.

- [ ] Create/prop-set with an unresolvable ref token → 400 naming property + token + expected format; nothing written.
- [ ] =--force= writes anyway (dangling lint still catches it later).
- [ ] Help documents the space-separated-ids format.
- [ ] Regression test reproducing the battle-test prose case end to end.

* DONE TASK-4WKNX FIX_SUBTASK closes straight to done, so a fix round that the goal requires to be reviewed cannot be dispatched a reviewer without a manual stage flip :cli:manager:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4WKNX
:PRIORITY: P2
:WRITE_SCOPE: crates/orgasmic-cli/**,crates/orgasmic-daemon/**
:END:

** Description
Found by running into it, 2026-08-05, closing TASK-YN5FJ.1.1.

=close_lifecycle_transitions= sends an implementer close to =Done= when the task
carries =:FIX_SUBTASK: t=, and to =InReview= otherwise. That encodes one-round
fix semantics, which the manager-dispatch convention states deliberately.

The ACTIVE GOAL says something else, and it is not reconcilable by reading
harder: "Fix subtasks minted from reviewer findings count as tasks: a BLOCK SHIP
is not closed until its fix round lands and passes a fresh review."

So for a fix round minted from a BLOCK SHIP, the two rules point opposite ways.
What happens in practice: =dispatch-close= flips the task to =done=, and the
reviewer dispatch then refuses with

: task TASK-YN5FJ.1.1 is in lifecycle stage done; reviewer dispatch is allowed only from IN_REVIEW

The refusal is CORRECT — a done task should not accept a reviewer. The defect is
upstream: the close had no way to say "this fix round still owes a review", so the
manager has to flip =done= -> =in_review= by hand afterwards to get the review the
goal demands. A state the board cannot express is a state managers will fake.

** Why this matters beyond one flip
The manual flip records a =task.state_transitioned= that reads like a correction,
not like policy. Anyone auditing later sees a task moved backwards out of done
with no way to tell whether that was process or panic. And a manager who does NOT
know the goal clause will simply not review the fix round at all — the tooling
actively steers them away from it.

** Fix directions, not yet decided
1. Let the close say it: a flag on =dispatch-close= (or a property on the task)
   that means "fix round, still owes review", so the close lands =in_review=
   without the manual flip.
2. Or derive it: a fix subtask minted from a reviewer finding labelled BLOCK SHIP
   goes to =in_review=; one minted from a non-blocking finding goes to =done=.
   That matches the goal clause exactly and needs no new operator input, but it
   requires the finding severity to be recorded somewhere the close can read —
   today it is prose in the reviewer report.
3. Or change the convention and the goal to agree on one rule. Cheapest, and it
   is a real option: decide that one-round fix semantics win and the goal clause
   is wrong.

Pick deliberately; do not implement all three.

** Acceptance
- A fix round minted from a BLOCK SHIP reaches its reviewer without a manual
  backwards stage transition.
- Whatever rule is chosen is stated in ONE place that both the convention and the
  close read from, so the next manager cannot find two answers.
- Existing one-round fix behaviour for non-blocking fix subtasks is preserved or
  its removal is explicit.
** Evidence
Landed =2d9d8b8= (merge) on main. Implementer: =implementer-claude-tmux= (tmux / claude / claude-opus-5 / high), run =run-20260805T184048-efc1a81d6ebb47439ce722ca7b4edbc2=, started_tx =tx-20260805-orgasmic-4519=.

THE MANAGER RULED THE POLICY, THE IMPLEMENTER CHOSE THE MECHANISM, and the split held. A =FIX_SUBTASK= implementer close now lands =in_review= like any other; the opt-out is =--fix-round-final=, which requires =--reason= and stamps =FIX_ROUND_FINAL=true= on the close tx.

THE RULING WAS MADE ON THIS SESSION OWN EVIDENCE, not taste. Five fix rounds ran 2026-08-05. One of them — TASK-M47E5.2, the fix round for three data-loss findings — was itself REJECTED with three MORE BLOCK SHIP findings, two P0. Under the old default it would have closed straight to =done= and six confirmed defects would be sitting on main unreviewed. The only thing that caught it was the manager flipping =done= -> =in_review= by hand, three separate times in one day, which nobody who had not read the goal would know to do. The asymmetry decides it: the old default fails as "a fix for a data-loss finding lands unreviewed"; the new one fails as "a trivial fix waits for a cheap review".

THREE IMPLEMENTER DECISIONS, all defensible and all stated:
- A FLAG, NOT A TASK PROPERTY. A property would describe the task forever, when what is recorded is a judgement about ONE round outcome, made at close time by the manager who read the diff.
- NAMED =--fix-round-final=, NOT another =--no-*=. The brief warned the two bypasses must not read as one concept; a near-homonym of =--no-review-required= would have invited exactly that. The flag names the state of the round rather than negating the word "review".
- REASON REQUIRED. Stronger here than for =--no-review-required=: this bypass is INVISIBLE IN THE OUTCOME — a task at =done= looks identical whether it was reviewed or declared not to need it — so the ledger has to carry the difference.

THE RULE NOW LIVES IN ONE PLACE: =implementer_done_stage(fix_subtask, fix_round_final)=, a four-row table with a unit test enumerating all four rows. =close_lifecycle_transitions= encodes nothing itself. Both shipped docs describe it by NAMING the flag, and =cli_parity= resolves shipped invocations against the real binary, so prose that lags the code is a gate failure.

A SECOND SHIPPED FILE WAS EDITED OUTSIDE THE DECLARED WRITE SCOPE, DECLARED RATHER THAN BURIED, and the manager accepts it: =shipped/schema/state-machine.org= still restated the old mapping ("transitions IN_PROGRESS -> DONE"). Leaving it would have preserved exactly the two-answers state this task acceptance forbids, so fixing it was the task, not scope creep.

Integration gates, re-run by the manager on the MERGED tree: =scripts/run-tests.sh -p orgasmic-cli= GREEN 0 failures; =cli_parity= 3 passed; =cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings= exit 0; =cargo fmt --all --check= exit 0; =orgasmic verify TASK-4WKNX= PASS.

THE INJECTION PROOF PINS THE END-TO-END SYMPTOM, NOT THE STAGE. The test reads the stage into a variable and lets the REVIEWER DISPATCH be the first assertion allowed to fail, so the pinned red is =task TASK-FIX-DECL is in lifecycle stage done; reviewer dispatch is allowed only from IN_REVIEW= — the thing an operator actually hits. Verified by the manager: exactly ONE panic in the red log, and it is that one. A proof pinned on the stage assertion would have passed while the workflow stayed broken.
** Review round 1 — REJECT (confirmed)
Reviewer `reviewer-codex-tmux` (tmux/codex/gpt-5.6-sol/high) on merge `2d9d8b8` vs first parent `a4199ed`. Verdict REJECT, one BLOCK SHIP. Manager confirmed the finding against the code rather than taking it on report, and found a third instance the reviewer did not.

**Confirmed — the new audit key is spoofable through the generic `--property` channel.**

`close_done_request` pushes caller properties (manager.rs:4718-4720) BEFORE it pushes the typed key (manager.rs:4726), and `parse_close_property` (:7183) accepts any uppercase key. Two concrete failures, both traced through the code path end to end:

1. `--property FIX_ROUND_FINAL=true` with no `--fix-round-final`: `validate_fix_round_final` returns `Ok` on its first line (`if !args.fix_round_final`), so neither `--reason` nor the `:FIX_SUBTASK:` check runs. The tx is stamped as a declared-final round; the task actually lands `in_review`. The ledger says one thing, the state machine did another.
2. `--fix-round-final --property FIX_ROUND_FINAL=false --reason <why>`: both land as duplicate keys. `extra()` (:7027) is `.find()` — FIRST-wins — so a reader sees `false` while the close really went to `done`.

Note the asymmetry that makes this easy to miss: `close_property_value` (:5790) reads ARGS last-wins (`.rev()`), while `extra()` reads the TX first-wins. The two readers disagree about which duplicate is authoritative.

**Why this is BLOCK SHIP and not a nit.** The entire argument for requiring `--reason` was that this bypass is invisible in the outcome — a `done` task looks identical whether it was reviewed or declared not to need review — so the ledger has to carry the difference. An audit key any caller can forge, without the reason the design demands, does not carry it. And this is the same shape already fenced for `VERDICT` under TASK-YN5FJ.1 RULING 3, decided hours earlier: a new key of the same class shipped without the fence its sibling has.

**Third instance, not in the report: `NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED` has the identical hole** (manager.rs:4720). `--property NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED=true` stamps the default-branch-gate bypass on the ledger while skipping the `--reason` that `--no-review-required` requires. That one is PRE-EXISTING, not introduced here — which is why the fix should be a reserved-key rule covering the class, not a one-off for `FIX_ROUND_FINAL`.

**Mitigating, and stated so the fix is not over-scoped:** nothing READS either key today; both are write-only ledger records. This is a false-record defect, not a live workflow break.

**Accepted from the review, no action:**
- `implementer_done_stage` is genuinely single-source in executable code; repository search found no surviving copy of the old mapping.
- `validate_fix_round_final` runs before run release, worktree cleanup, close-tx append, and lifecycle mutation. (The reviewer noted `reconcile_torn_closes_best_effort` still precedes all close validation — deliberate TASK-EP3H1 behaviour, repairing an unrelated owed close, not a regression. Agreed.)
- `--fix-round-final` and `--no-review-required` are coherent together: distinct gates, distinct keys.
- Both shipped doctrine files match the code; no third file states the old rule.
- Independent re-verification by the reviewer: `orgasmic verify TASK-4WKNX` PASS, `cli_parity` 3 passed.

**Deferred, not folded in:** the reviewer suggests a close-time next-action line or a `dispatch-status` diagnostic for a `FIX_SUBTASK` parked `in_review` with no reviewer dispatch. That is a usability follow-up on a workflow that now works; it does not belong in a fix round for an audit hole.
** Follow-up filed from the review's Open Questions
The reviewer's second open question — a close-time next-action line or a =dispatch-status= diagnostic for a =FIX_SUBTASK= parked =in_review= with no reviewer dispatch — is filed as TASK-3HR8R, and it was UPGRADED from the usability follow-up the manager first called it.

A board-hygiene sweep the same day found TASK-M47E5.1 merged at 18:09 and never reviewed, stalled in exactly this shape. So the reviewer reasoned FORWARD from a design change and the sweep reasoned BACKWARD from a real miss, and both landed on the same gap. It is a review the goal requires going missing silently, not polish.

** Description

Fix round for the one BLOCK SHIP on TASK-4WKNX's review, confirmed by the manager
against the code. The full mechanism is on the parent under "Review round 1 —
REJECT (confirmed)"; read it there rather than re-deriving it.

In one line: ~close_done_request~ pushes caller ~--property~ entries before it
pushes its own typed keys, and ~parse_close_property~ accepts any uppercase key,
so a bypass-audit key can be forged or contradicted by the caller it is meant to
audit.

** The class, not the instance

The reviewer found it on ~FIX_ROUND_FINAL~. The manager found the same hole on
~NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED~ (manager.rs:4720), which is PRE-EXISTING — 4WKNX did not
introduce it, it introduced a second instance of it. ~VERDICT~ is the only key of
this class currently fenced (TASK-YN5FJ.1 RULING 3), and it is fenced by a
hand-written one-off ~if let (Some, Some)~ pair.

Three keys, two unfenced, one bespoke fence: the fix is a rule about
manager-owned tx keys, not a third copy of the same ~if~.

** Acceptance

- A caller cannot forge or contradict any manager-owned close-tx key through
  ~--property~. Covers at minimum ~FIX_ROUND_FINAL~, ~NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED~ and
  ~VERDICT~.
- ~VERDICT~'s existing behaviour is preserved exactly: ~--property VERDICT=~ is a
  supported legacy free-text spelling and must keep working alone, while
  flag-plus-property still refuses by name. Whatever rule replaces the one-off
  must reproduce this, not flatten it.
- The refusal happens with the other early close refusals — before run release,
  worktree cleanup, and any tx append.
- Tests pin property-only forgery AND typed-flag/property collision on the
  production path, and assert the close was refused before the worktree was
  cleaned up.

** Not in scope

The reviewer's usability suggestion (a close-time next-action line, or a
~dispatch-status~ diagnostic for a ~FIX_SUBTASK~ parked ~in_review~ with no
reviewer dispatch). That is a follow-up on a workflow that now works. File it
separately if it earns a task.
** Landed and verified by the manager
** Review round 1 — REJECT (confirmed, and the severity is higher)
Reviewer =reviewer-codex-tmux= (tmux/codex/gpt-5.6-sol/high) on merge =caf06ae=
vs base =f60af0a=. Verdict REJECT, one BLOCK SHIP. Manager confirmed it against
the code and confirmed the severity is HIGHER than the report states.

=== The finding, confirmed

=MANAGER_OWNED_CLOSE_PROPERTIES= is a three-key denylist, not the class rule the
task asked for. =close_done_request= pushes caller properties (=:4751=) and THEN
appends manager-derived structural keys — =CLOSED_TX= (=:4763=),
=push_lifecycle_extra=, =push_cleanup_extra=, =GOAL_ID= — none of which are in
the table. With =extra()= first-wins, the caller's forged value is the one every
reader sees.

=== Why this is worse than the report says: these keys are CONSUMED

The report frames the risk as forged audit data. Manager checked the consumers
and it is not only audit:

- =close_matching_dispatch= (=:7033=) selects WHICH open dispatch record a close
  terminates by matching =CLOSED_TX=. A forged value marks the WRONG generation
  closed and leaves the real one open.
- =close_tx_ran_cleanup= (=:7059=) sets =record.cleanup_already_run= from
  =CLEANUP_STATUS=. A forged =ok= makes a close that never ran cleanup look like
  it did — and cleanup is the path that SALVAGES uncommitted worker output before
  removing a worktree. This project has already destroyed a worker's work once
  (TASK-2BPWM, TASK-D0GA3).
- =cleanup_status_reports_failure= (=:7158=) scans the ledger for cleanup
  failures; a forged =ok= hides a real one from that report.

So the vector is state corruption and suppressed salvage, not a false record.
BLOCK SHIP stands and the severity is right.

=== This is MY scoping failure, not the implementer's

The round-2 brief said "a rule about manager-owned close-tx keys, not a third
copy of the same =if=" — and then named exactly three keys, in a table, in the
brief's own markdown. The implementer built precisely what was described. The
table it produced is good work: the =const fn reserved(...)= default and the
verbatim =VERDICT= text are both right and both survive into round 3. What was
missing was in the specification.

=== The structural answer, found while verifying

*Every tx-extra reader in the workspace is first-wins.* Verified:
=manager.rs:7101=, =crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/index.rs:2008=, and the assertion
helpers — all =.iter().find(...)=. No last-wins reader exists.

So pushing the manager's own extras BEFORE the caller's =--property= loop makes
every forged duplicate INERT for consumption, for every manager-owned key
including ones nobody has written yet, with no list to maintain and no drift to
detect. That is the property the acceptance actually wants and it costs a
reorder.

It is not sufficient alone, and saying why matters: an inert duplicate still sits
in the ledger where a human reads it, and for the three deliberate bypass keys a
silent no-op is the wrong answer — forging =FIX_ROUND_FINAL= should be a loud
refusal, not a shrug. Hence two layers in round 3.

=== Accepted from the review, no action

- Placement verified independently: validation at =:1010= precedes merge
  verification (=:1022=), reservation/release (=:1096=), cleanup (=:1163=), tx
  append (=:1201=) and lifecycle mutation; the only mutating call before it is
  the explicitly accepted =reconcile_torn_closes_best_effort=.
- =VERDICT= collision text is byte-for-byte identical to base =f60af0a:969-971=;
  =reviewer_done_stage= and =close_verdict_value= unchanged, still reading either
  spelling. Independently exercised typed-only, property-only and collision.
- Duplicate handling for the three listed keys is sound: the =Reserved= arm
  refuses regardless of value, so duplicates cannot slip past.
- =parse_close_property= rejects lower-case, padded and non-ASCII-uppercase keys.

=== The =NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED= judgement is SETTLED, with a better argument

The brief asked for a real opinion including "the author was wrong". The reviewer
said Reserved is right and gave a stronger reason than the implementer's
absence-of-callers evidence: =project.org:12-18= records an explicit greenfield
bias — do not assume backward compatibility absent an explicit requirement.
And unlike =VERDICT=, whose property form preserves free-text values outside the
typed enum, a =NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED= alias adds no vocabulary and no capability
except bypassing the mandatory reason. Reserved, and the reasoning is now on the
record instead of in a report.

** Description

Round 3 on the manager-owned close-tx key namespace. The finding and its
confirmed mechanism are on TASK-4WKNX.1 under "Review round 1 — REJECT
(confirmed, and the severity is higher)". Read it there; do not re-derive it.

In one line: =MANAGER_OWNED_CLOSE_PROPERTIES= names three keys, but
=close_done_request= appends =CLOSED_TX=, =LIFECYCLE_FROM=/=LIFECYCLE_TO=,
=CLEANUP_STATUS=, =SALVAGE_*= and =GOAL_ID= AFTER the caller's =--property=
loop — and =extra()= is first-wins, so a forged caller value is the one every
reader sees.

** These keys are consumed, so this is not an audit problem

- =close_matching_dispatch= (=manager.rs:7033=) picks WHICH open dispatch a close
  terminates from =CLOSED_TX=.
- =close_tx_ran_cleanup= (=:7059=) sets =cleanup_already_run= from
  =CLEANUP_STATUS= — and cleanup is the path that SALVAGES uncommitted worker
  output before removing a worktree.
- =cleanup_status_reports_failure= (=:7158=) scans for cleanup failures a forged
  =ok= would hide.

** The ruling: two layers, and neither alone is sufficient

*Layer 1 — ordering, which covers keys nobody has written yet.* Push the
manager's own extras BEFORE the caller's =--property= loop. Measured and
verified by the manager: EVERY tx-extra reader in the workspace is first-wins
(=manager.rs:7101=, =crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/index.rs:2008=, and the test
helpers) — there is no last-wins reader. So manager-first makes a forged
duplicate inert for consumption, for every key including future ones, with no
list to maintain.

*Layer 2 — refusal, which covers the deliberate bypass keys.* Ordering alone is
not enough and the reason is not cosmetic: an inert duplicate still sits in the
ledger where a person reads it, and for =FIX_ROUND_FINAL= / =NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED=
a silent no-op is the wrong answer. Forging a bypass key should be a loud
refusal.

*Explicitly rejected: extending the denylist to enumerate every structural key.*
That is a longer list with the same defect — a new key is protected only if
someone remembers to add it, which is precisely what this round exists to fix.

** Keep, do not rebuild

The round-2 work is good and most of it survives: the =const fn reserved(...)=
default, the =AliasedVerdict= exception, the byte-identical =VERDICT= refusal
text, the placement before release/cleanup/append/mutation, and the production
tests. This round changes the SHAPE of the coverage, not the policy.

** Acceptance

- A manager-owned key added in future is protected WITHOUT being added to any
  list, and a test demonstrates that rather than asserting it in prose.
- Forging =CLOSED_TX= or =CLEANUP_STATUS= through =--property= cannot change what
  =close_matching_dispatch= or =close_tx_ran_cleanup= decide.
- =FIX_ROUND_FINAL= and =NO_REVIEW_REQUIRED= still refuse loudly, before run
  release, worktree cleanup, tx append and lifecycle mutation.
- =VERDICT='s three behaviours are unchanged and its refusal text stays
  byte-identical: property-only accepted, typed-only accepted, both refused.
- An injection proof pinning a CONSUMED key, not just a refused one.

** Not in scope

TASK-3HR8R (the parked-=in_review= diagnostic). The reviewer re-confirmed it is
out of scope here.

* DONE TASK-4YC8E hermes reasoning_effort alias collides with the daemon's dual-key driver_config :drivers:bug:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4YC8E
:PRIORITY: P1
:END:

`adapters/hermes.rs` declares

    #[serde(default, alias = "effort")]
    reasoning_effort: Option<String>

while the daemon writes the value under BOTH keys at once (`api.rs`:
`"effort": effort` and `"reasoning_effort": reasoning_effort`, lines 3573-3574;
also 2329-2330). Serde then sees one field populated twice and fails
deserialization, so `validate_config` returns `InvalidConfig` and the dispatch
dies with

    400 Bad Request: {"error":"driver configuration is invalid"}

Measured on claude 2026-07-26: adding that exact alias to `ClaudeAcpConfig`
reproduced this immediately, and removing it fixed it. Hermes carries the alias
today, so a hermes dispatch that sets an effort should fail the same way.

NOT VERIFIED for hermes itself — inferred from identical code and a reproduced
failure in a sibling adapter, not from a hermes dispatch. Confirm before fixing:
run a hermes acp-stdio dispatch with `--effort high` and check for the 400.

If confirmed the fix is one line — drop `alias = "effort"`, since the daemon
already writes `reasoning_effort`. Check codex too; it also carries
`reasoning_effort` and needs the same read.

Worth fixing beyond the crash: the error text names neither the field nor the
adapter. `InvalidConfig(e.to_string())` has serde's message in hand and drops it
on the floor at the API boundary. Surfacing it would have made this a ten-second
diagnosis instead of a grep through api.rs.

The dual-key write is itself questionable — one value under two names is what
made an ordinary alias a landmine. Consider emitting only `reasoning_effort`
once every adapter reads that key.

* DONE TASK-4YX1K Default to proceeding; confirm only for irreversible or outward-facing actions :workflow:runtime:process:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-4YX1K
:DEPENDS_ON: TASK-YGB1R
:PRIORITY:   P1
:END:

Problem: the runtime tells a manager what work to do and how much process to apply, but says nothing about when to stop and ask a human. Agents fill that vacuum with timidity. Observed 2026-07-25: a manager finished TASK-KWSTJ, correctly identified that a reviewer cannot see uncommitted source, and then asked the user for permission to commit to a local branch — a reversible, machine-local step that was already the precondition for a review the user had asked for. The question contained no decision. It cost a round-trip and stalled the work.

This is the mirror image of TASK-3CM0Q. That task stops an agent from silently proceeding through a decision that is genuinely the user's. This one stops an agent from interrupting on something that is not a decision at all. An agent without an explicit line between them oscillates: the same session skipped a real tier decision, was corrected, then over-corrected into asking about a mechanical step. Both failures are the human checkpoint landing in the wrong place, and neither is fixed by telling the agent to "use judgement".

Work:
1. State the default in `shipped/entry/router.org` and `shipped/workflows/default.org`: proceed. Asking is the exception and needs a reason that names which property of the action triggers it.
2. Define confirmation triggers by property, not by feeling. Confirm when an action is hard to reverse, leaves the machine, or spends someone else's resources — pushing to a remote, publishing a release or artifact, force-pushing or rewriting history, deleting or rewriting operator session/run history, touching the LaunchAgent or a live production daemon, or anything that mutates a shared or external service.
3. Name the proceed class just as explicitly, because a bare "proceed by default" will not survive contact with a cautious agent: committing to a local branch, creating and removing worktrees, running gates and test suites, reading anything, and `.orgasmic/` state writes through the CLI.
4. Cover the standing-authorization case: once a user has approved a plan, the mechanical steps that plan obviously entails do not each need their own approval. Re-asking inside an approved plan is itself the defect.
5. Say what to do instead of asking when an agent is unsure but the action is in the proceed class: act, then report what was done plainly enough to be reversed.

Non-goal: expanding autonomy on the confirm class. This narrows *where* the human is asked, it does not reduce *whether* they are asked about the things that matter.

Acceptance:
- committing to a branch, creating a worktree, or running gates never produces a permission question
- pushing, publishing, force-pushing, or touching the live daemon still does
- the router text distinguishes the two classes by a stated property, so an agent reaching an unlisted action can classify it rather than guess
- reads coherently against TASK-3CM0Q: one task puts a checkpoint where a decision exists, this one removes checkpoints where none does

* DONE TASK-547MT dispatch-wait 503 claim_store_unreadable because ~/.orgasmic/state/recovery-claims did not exist; a lost wait must say worker state unknown :vscode-orsl-letter:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-547MT
:PRIORITY: P1
:END:

** Description
Source: vscode-orsl manager letter 2026-08-22 (operator-forwarded, 40 dispatches over 4 days, orgasmic 0.0.18). Item 9. `dispatch-wait` returned 503 `claim_store_unreadable`; cause: `~/.orgasmic/state/recovery-claims/` missing. mkdir -p + chmod made it intermittent. Every dead wait had to be re-checked with dispatch-status.
Code: crates/orgasmic-daemon/src/recovery_claim.rs read path.
** Expected
- The daemon creates every directory it reads (missing claim dir == empty store, created on first use).
- A wait that loses its connection prints `wait lost — worker state unknown, re-run dispatch-status` and exits non-zero distinct from run-ended.
** Acceptance
- Test: claim store read on a fresh HOME returns empty, not 503; CLI message on connection loss.
** Resolution
Root cause of the 503: the claim store opens `~/.orgasmic/state` and `recovery-claims` via openat; with the daemon at the 256-fd ceiling that open fails EMFILE, which classifies as Unobserved → claim_store_unreadable (an absent recovery-claims dir is already read as an empty store, and Home::ensure creates state/ at boot). Fixed by the fd-leak fix 8bd8287. (b) shipped in 5033cce: a failed dispatch-wait request prints "dispatch-wait lost … worker state unknown, not ended; re-run dispatch-status".

* DONE TASK-567JG Respawn dispatch completion watcher on boot reattach (no last.txt after daemon restart) :daemon:dispatch:reattach:
:PROPERTIES:
:ID: TASK-567JG
:SEVERITY: medium
:END:

Distinct second failure mode discovered while fixing TASK-B05AM (the stall-clobber, fixed in ed6a6fc). When the daemon restarts MID-RUN, the run is reattached (boot reconciliation, api::reattach_live_runs_on_boot) but the dispatch completion watcher — a tokio task spawned only at dispatch time (api.rs spawn_dispatch_completion_watcher, called only from the dispatch handler ~3453) — died with the old daemon process. No watcher is respawned for the reattached run, so when it later releases, write_dispatch_completion_artifacts is never called and NEITHER last.txt NOR stdout.log is written. Observed on TASK-Y2ZQJ (session had a 'reattach' lifecycle event; 15053 assistant chunks + run_complete present, yet no last.txt).

Root cause: the session's RunMeta lifecycle event carries transport/harness/project_id/worktree/driver_config but NOT last_path/stdout_path (the dispatch artifact paths, derived CLI-side from the brief filename stem). So on reattach the daemon cannot reconstruct where to write the artifacts.

Fix direction: persist last_path + stdout_path (and worktree_path) in the RunMeta lifecycle event at dispatch time; on boot reattach (reattach_live_runs_on_boot), reconstruct a DispatchCompletion from RunMeta and call spawn_dispatch_completion_watcher for each reattached worker/reviewer run. Add a test: reattach a run with RunMeta artifact paths, release it, assert last.txt is written. Until then, the harness transcript remains the rescue source for restart-mid-run dispatches.

Workaround already in effect: prefer in-process agent reviewers over rmux dispatches while the report path is fragile; rescue from harness transcript when a dispatch loses its report.
** Evidence

The empty-git-remote-under-load flake class: three test names, one shape, no

   TASK-0RCRY full-workspace run, 2026-07-29.
2. `post_projects_scaffolds_and_registers_uninitialized_project`
   (integration.rs:437) — same shape, right: "git@example.com:org/fresh.git" —
   same run.
3. `index::tests::live_rebuild_preserves_repo_url_and_schedules_post_bind_refresh`
   — the already-documented candidate in verify/flake-registry.toml's notes;
   TASK-5FEN5 fixed its test-side wait (drive the probe until the URL lands),
   so THIS sighting class is about the remaining callers of the same
   under-load-git-probe behaviour, not that fixed test.

Shape: `refresh_repo_url` bounds its `git config --get remote.origin.url`
probe (3s) and returns WITHOUT WRITING when the bound is spent — deliberate
production behaviour with its own test. Under load the probe loses the race and

on a loaded machine — the failures are that distribution's tail.

=== Ask

Per the 5FEN5 standard: reproduce under load, then fix each observer at the
synchronization (wait on the probe's completion, or drive until present with a
hang-guard bound), not the budget size. integration.rs tests are out-of-process
observers — check what completion signal they CAN see before designing.
Registering with this task as owner is the fallback; fixing is the goal.

=== Acceptance

- Either the named tests survive >=5 consecutive loaded runs post-fix (pre-fix
  counts pinned), or they are registered with measured signatures and the
  diagnosis documented.
- Injection per TCTTD standard where patch-expressible (the 5FEN5 artifact's
  first-probe-returns-empty injection is the template).
